utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning. Good morning to the technical booth. Good morning to the interpreters, representatives of the registry. Good morning, counsel for the Prosecution, for the Defence. Let us continue with our work today, that is, with the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka. Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Somers: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, tell us, please, when you first met Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he would come to the Omarska camp. That was the first time I saw him live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of him prior to seeing him live?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I heard that after the takeover he became the chief of the Public Security Station, that is, the chief of police for the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did he replace when he became -- or when he came to that position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talundzic, if you mean him, was a Muslim, and Drljaca was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of Mr. Drljaca's relationship to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard therefore that he had become the chief of the Public Security Station, and when he came to Omarska, I saw him on two occasions, if my memory serves me right. A driver would also come, Radovan Vokic who was chief's driver and a long-time policeman whom I knew, and I probably talked to Vokic on those occasions, so it became clear to me that that was the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions during proceedings here, we have discussed and have seen a document that was dated 31st of May, 1992, signed by Simo Drljaca, which effectively sets up Omarska camp. Do you remember our discussing that document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I also said that I saw this document here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you may not have seen the document before coming before this Tribunal, were you made aware of its contents, the various provisions in the document before you went to work at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And while we're doing this, if I might ask the usher kindly to put 2/4.11 on the ELMO. We can use our copy if you'd like. I won't distribute it again, but I think it would be helpful to have it in front of the witness. That is the document to which we were referring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question to you was, although you may not have seen this document before coming here, were you made aware of its contents, the various provisions in the document, before you went to work at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never learned anything about its contents, and when the document was shown here during the proceedings, it became clear to me that one of the paragraphs which was conveyed to us by Zeljko Meakic is actually contained in this document. The paragraph concerns the work that was to be done by the police, so that is actually the only connection that I could make, could establish with the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which paragraph would that be in this document? Could you point it out and perhaps take a second to read it to us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to have a look at the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's paragraph 6, because Zeljko told us that the duty of us policemen from Omarska would be to provide security to the collection centre, as it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was your understanding -- well, did you find out about this before you actually physically went to work there, or when did you find out about the information that's contained in paragraph 6? When did Zeljko tell you this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One to two days after we started working, that is, after the investigations centre opened. Two days went by and then Zeljko told us that we had certain duties which were regulated in some kind of order, from which I can conclude that Zeljko must have seen such a document or must have been told about it by someone. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zeljko also tell you that part of the duties would then be to prevent escape? Escape.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every policeman who was involved in regular police work knew about it, and Zeljko emphasised it as well, that one of the duties of the police was to prevent escape, which implied also preventing, if possible and necessary, any attack on the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to just clarify. When you said Zeljko emphasised it, do you mean in connection with the work at Omarska camp he emphasised that that would be one of the tasks? Preventing escape in connection with Omarska camp, he emphasised that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pass this on to the guards who worked at Omarska camp with you, or did he pass it on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Zeljko told to all of us together. I cannot recall that he gathered us together or that he talked to groups of people, or maybe he told this to an oncoming shift, when they would come on duty. He said that the shift which gathered in the village of Omarska before going to work had been told about such orders by him. So he emphasised it once again and drew our attention to cases of intensified activity, that is, the need to intensify security and prevent escape. The mere prevention of escape is self-implied and understood. It is possible that the reserve policemen didn't know, were not aware of it. But I didn't have to be told specifically about it because, from my previous experience, I knew that that would be one of our duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that suggest, though, if this was two days after you arrived for your work at Omarska, that there were two days when you did not know what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. However, I have to say once again what I said yesterday. When people from Banja Luka were leaving, then their superior officer told them and every one of us that there were detainees there and that one of our basic duties was to prevent escape; and that for any further or other types of duties or work, that we would be given appropriate instructions from our superiors. They were trying to get away as soon as possible, the unit that was from Banja Luka. That is what we heard afterwards. The fact that they were from Banja Luka, that is what we learnt later on. Those whom I had seen were all dressed in camouflage uniforms, which I saw on that occasion for the first time. Those uniforms were not normally used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you remind us, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you remind us, please, the name of the superior officer to whom you were referring from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot do that, really. We didn't see each other for longer than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about preventing escape or preventing anyone from coming in, is it your understanding that that also contemplates preventing an attack on the detainees, on the prisoners? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you're asking me personally, yes, that was the kind of understanding that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there any distinction made in your instructions as to by whom that attack might be made, whether it was a force from the outside or a force from the inside, an attack on prisoners? What was your understanding of that instruction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood was that it referred from someone from -- to someone from the outside because there was no possibility of any such attack on prisoners from the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what if a guard attacked a prisoner on the inside? Would that be any less of an attack on a prisoner in your mind as a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A guard or a policeman -- that is to say, the situation was such that it was understood that a guard could not attack or assault a prisoner, that he couldn't nor wouldn't do it. So no specific mention was made of that possibility. I don't quite understand what you mean. Do you mean that those who were guarding the prisoners were supposed to have someone else guarding them in order to prevent guards from assaulting the prisoners? I don't know exactly how you mean that. It was implied that, self-understood that a guard would never attack a prisoner. Prisoners were to be protected by the guards from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was understood that a guard -- I want to make sure I get your words correct. "The situation was such that it was understood that a guard could not attack or assault a prisoner." Help us understand - we were not there - help us understand how it was understood.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a common understanding as regards the work of the police. The police are supposed to protect citizens from other citizens. Now, we should perhaps ask ourselves, who is supposed to protect the citizens if they come under an attack of the police? That is why I'm saying that it was understood and implied. In view of my experience as a policeman, it was always my duty as a policeman to protect citizens from the attack of other citizens, so I, of course, understood that that would be the behaviour of my colleagues as well, that they would be protecting citizens from attack of other citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other citizens could include police officers or -- whether reserve or active duty or somebody acting as a guard, those are citizens also, aren't they, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are all citizens, only some of us are policemen and some are detainees, but both detainees and policeman are citizens. I don't understand what you mean. At that moment the policemen were policemen. In addition to that, they were also citizens, but when they're on duty as police officers, then they cannot be considered as ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself just raised a question and said, "Now, we should perhaps ask ourselves, who is supposed to protect the citizens if they come under an attack of the police? That is why I'm saying that it was understood and implied." Well, how -- you tell us how you view that. How do you protect a citizen, how do you protect a citizen who at that moment comes under the attack by a policeperson? Reserve, active duty, immaterial. What would you do as a long-standing, experienced, professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I explain this to you? There was no provision in any of the regulations which would explicitly govern and prescribe a special service which would be in charge of protecting citizens from an assault of the police. That is one thing. In the system in which we lived, it was believed that the police simply could not attack citizens. Now, if this should happen, then in that case there are several possibilities. I spoke about that yesterday to a certain extent. If we interpret the rules literally, if such an incident should happen before my own eyes, if a policeman should attack a citizen, then I would intervene, of course. However, certain qualifications need to be made here. If a policeman should slap a citizen, in that case I should perhaps ask myself about the authority that I have to intervene or not. In that case, I think that I would have an obligation to report about that to my superiors. Second, if the violation of human rights in question is a drastic one, if it's an attempt of murder or some other kind of ill-treatment, then speaking for myself, I'm sure I would try to prevent it if, of course, it is happening before my eyes, in my physical presence. In that case, of course I would try to prevent it. In that case, I think I can intervene, that is, I think I will -- would intervene, although later on I run the risk of having problems with the policeman in question. Then you would probably have a conflict of interest. He would probably think that he has the right to do that and authority to do that, and I will probably think that he does not have such an authority, and then we would probably have a conflict between the two of us. But personally, I think I would always intervene in cases of murder attempt, ill-treatment, and similar incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were working back in the former Yugoslav, let's say when you were working in Prijedor during peacetime, did you work on the streets as a street cop, as we say? Did you work on the streets, patrol?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for three years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry a weapon? Did you carry a sidearm?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose in your carrying that weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main purpose was to protect life of citizens, on condition, and those are very strict regulations, that such an attack cannot be prevented in any other way. That is, if an attack on a citizen cannot be prevented in any other way, an attack which is likely to endanger the citizen' life, then in that case the policeman is entitled to use his weapon according to very strict regulations governing its use. There is a caveat, of course, with this rule, which says that if the attack cannot be prevented in any other way, so that was a kind of last resort in such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your experience on the street, I'd like to give you a scenario and you can tell me how you feel the appropriate response should be described. You're in Prijedor, bright sunny day, peacetime, and across the street you notice a man with a gun coming up behind an old lady carrying her groceries, and he sticks the gun in her face and says, "Give me your purse or I'll kill you." And it looks like he's going to kill her. What do you do in that instance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You yourself said that it was a scenario. I have to say that I never had that kind of scenario during my work, but I can perhaps use my imagination and think about it a little bit. First of all, I think that the person in question should -- would have to be an exceptional marksman, and I would have to think that this potential perpetrator would effectively use the weapon. This may be only a threat, of course, but I have to be 100 per cent sure also that the weapon in question is a real one, because you can always have a fake gun, a plastic pistol, which is used only for purposes of intimidation of the person who is supposed to be intimidated. So all that knowledge would have to be necessary for me in that particular moment. I would also have to be very sure about the distance. If I'm not a very good marksman, I can end up killing the woman and not the assaulter. I also have to know whether there are any other citizens in the vicinity because the use of firearms by the policeman is strictly prohibited in a crowd, regardless of what is going on, except for shooting in the air for purposes of intimidation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same scenario, the guy with the gun fires off three rounds to let the old lady know he's not joking. You're satisfied it's a real gun and he's probably going to do some damage to her. What do you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I would use the firearm as well. But I can only say that it is possible. I cannot give you any more specific answer. We would have to have the appropriate scenario, of course. Because, again, as I said, I never had -- I was never faced with such a scenario before the war. Or difficulties that I had, I was able to resolve in a better way. I only had two classical police interventions during my career. Everything else was dealt with through conversation. One such occasion was when I was attacked with a broken glass, when I was a very young policeman, by someone, and there was another incident later on. I no longer remember what it was. It was only in 1994 that I handcuffed a person. So after 20 years of experience, that was the first time that I actually had to handcuff someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fellow with the glass who, I think you said -- let me make sure I have that correct. The fellow who attacked you with a broken glass, did he have a weapon, a handgun also, or was the only weapon his glass?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have a firearm. He just had this piece of bottle which is broken in -- you know, like they do it in a bar, and then he ends up holding the upper part of the broken bottle in his hand as a weapon. There is a regulation which says that the attack need not be an attack with a firearm. It can be with some other type of -- similar type of object. You can be attacked with an axe, a knife, or some other appropriate object for inflicting physical injuries which are of a more serious or fatal nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I understand you correctly, you talked this down. You essentially negotiated yourself out of a potentially dangerous situation; is that what you're telling us? Your negotiation skills were what brought you through that safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, there were no complicated interventions on my part except for this one. But I have to go back to the Rules of Service which explicitly state that those things can be done if nothing else can be done to prevent the attack. The weapon is always the last resort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your own relationship, going back for a moment to Simo Drljaca -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] For the record, the use of truncheon or a club is not entered in the transcript. The witness said that before the use of a weapon, one classical object that can be used is a police bat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, could you please clarify this with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Simic is referring to page number 11, line 12 or 13, more or less -- or 16 and 17. I think at least that that was the interpretation that I received which corresponds to what I can see in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, because there seems to be a question, would you describe -- going in escalation of use of force, would you describe what you'd have to use in the way of weaponry before you would be allowed to use a firearm? What type of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before any such intervention, there is a kind of sequence that is followed. If the talks have fallen through, then you can always use physical force or a rubber baton; then you can use various means of restraint; and finally, if everything fails, then you can use a weapon, you can use a firearm, providing that all other conditions for the use of a firearm have been fulfilled. You have to know in advance what the person in question has done, if we talk about the criminal types of behaviour in general, if we are dealing with usual suspects, people who have already been suspected of various criminal offences. However, if you have a minor person who has robbed a kiosk and has in his possession a box of cigarettes and is trying to escape, then of course you're not going to use a firearm against him. That would only do more damage to the service than it would benefit the society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we agree that however you make this analysis which you have just given to us as a professional officer, it has to be made very, very quickly or else there could be a disastrous result for the intended victim; do you agree about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that such a decision has to be made quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your time in Omarska camp, how often did you find yourself having to make those quick decisions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the incident that we heard about at length during the proceedings when a person opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I do recall that, I'm sure. Did you have to make the same analysis when you went into the room from which you heard the screams and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the cries? I think your testimony was something like, and I have to paraphrase because I don't have it in front of me, but you were pretty nervous about going in that room, you were nervous for yourself. Did you do the analysis about what you would do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did. And what you -- and you concluded that that intervention was or was not warranted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, I couldn't analyse things in advance before seeing what was happening. Once I entered, there was no beating going on inside the room, so it was over, it had ended. So these are seconds that are in question. The offence had terminated so I had no reason to use force or a baton, to simplify things. Especially yesterday, we spent half a day talking about it, that it was inspectors I was dealing with, which was an additional consideration. So nothing was actually happening before my very eyes. If I had actually found the inspector or maybe a guard who was with him actually beating the person, the simplest thing for me to do would be to grab them by their arms and push them into the corner. That would be a more effective way of intervening than any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember in your interview with Mr. Bennett --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we could ask to have that perhaps put back on the ELMO, or if you have your copy, it's 3/201. I'm looking at the English translation, page 8, and I don't know how it's broken down in the B/C/S, but I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I think it is 3/203. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have 3/201 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're right. I'm sorry. My mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the article in front of you in your own language? It might be easier. Otherwise, if you're willing to accept the translation as we have it read out. But it's the actual interview from Slobodna Bosna. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the witness to be given the original text from Slobodna Bosna, because we had some problems yesterday with the interpretation of the interview with Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Simic, it is not the interview with Mr. Reid. We are talking about the newspaper article. They are two different things. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. But all we are asking is that Mr. Kvocka be given the original text so he can follow it, of the interview. He doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have -- is there an extra copy, Ms. Gustin, that we may be able to turn over? Otherwise, if we may put it on the ELMO and have it read out that would probably be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, now. So please continue. Mr. Simic, it was my mistake. I mixed the two up. When you mentioned Reid, it was the interview, but we're talking about the newspaper article. So I got it mixed up, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked on page 8, let me give you the language, Mr. Kvocka, maybe it will be helpful. Just before it there is a paragraph that mentions the "white house" and the "red house," if you can find it in Serbo-Croatian; otherwise, it's on the ELMO. I am looking at a passage where you were asked -- they were talking about the "white house" and the "red house," "Were people killed in those buildings?" Your answer was, "Not before my eyes."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still haven't found it. How does the question begin in the original, because that's why I can't find it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you how it's phrased there, but if you could listen for the translation; it's a very short sentence. "Were people killed in those buildings," referring to the "white house" and the "red house." And your answer, very short sentence, was, "Not before my eyes." I think you're being informed it's on 5, page 5. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, regarding this interview, we were discussing it yesterday, I never gave an interview to Mr. Chris Bennett. I gave an interview to the British television station ITN, as far as I can remember, Channel 4, with a gentleman called Roy Bob, Bob Roy. A gentleman from the International Crisis Staff was present. Whether he recorded that without my knowing, I don't know. These answers are quite possible. I'm not questioning them, but I'm never sure whether Mr. Chris Bennett conveyed everything accurately the way I said it. I'm simply not sure of that. I'm not saying that he didn't, and I don't think there's any problem. I'd be glad to answer any questions about it. But I want to tell you that I saw this interview for the first time when Mr. Dusko Tadic gave me a copy of this newspaper in the detention unit once I came here. It was never shown to me. Mr. Chris Bennett didn't put questions to me. He was not in charge of the interview. The questions were put by a reporter of this English television station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The article, nonetheless, that was relied upon by your own lawyer at your motion for provisional release, does ask that question. If you had been present during the time of some murders, if you were on the premises or if it were on your work hours, wherever you were supposed to be, is it really your position that if you're informed of, directly or indirectly, meaning you could even suspect it, that a murder has taken place on your watch, that if you didn't see it, there's nothing you can do about it? I mean, we know you can't bring the person back from the dead. What would you do about the fact that there was a murder?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a policeman, all information I gain, it is my duty to pass on to my immediate superior, and then also the further procedure is prescribed. My immediate superior also has no authority regarding the actual commission of a criminal offence. He does not have the authority to interfere. Murder is a very grave criminal offence, and it is only the crime department that can conduct an investigation. However, members of the police, of course, are not prohibited from passing on useful information in that connection. So this comes under the area of the investigation of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interfering. We've heard this already. I think Ms. Susan Somers' question was whether you would make a report on it or not. We know already the position of Mr. Kvocka, so please move on a little, if you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to point out, Judge Rodrigues is absolutely correct. I'm trying to find out, what would you do -- what did you do when all the murders that we have heard testimony about in this proceeding took place? What did you do about them? To whom did you pass on the reports? Where are the reports?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there's no allegation that I heard a report about that. The information that I did hear, I did pass on. During my work there, which was for I don't know how many shifts - it would be easy to calculate that - we had information that there was mistreatment of persons; that is, I could have heard such information from some guards and from some detainees. Each time I would pass on such information to Zeljko Meakic, and each time his response was that he was aware of it, that he had heard about it, but that he was unable to get closer to the sources of information. And what he did next, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, didn't you worry that if nothing was done about it, and you claim you passed the information on, that somebody higher up when they found out about it would say, "Why didn't that Kvocka pass the information on?" Wouldn't that have made you concerned that you might be blamed for failing to act according to your regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, no one is obligated to give me feedback information. There is no obligation to inform the policeman as to what a crime inspector has done. That is one point. Another is, if no one reproached me for anything, then it means that he never established that I had concealed anything. So if I had glossed over something in silence, then there would be disciplinary proceedings against me, if there were such a situation. This is all hypothetical, because there were no such reproaches against me why I had covered up something. Nobody said to me, "Kvocka, we have established that you knew about something and you didn't tell us about it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how many times were you interviewed as a witness in an investigation by the investigating authorities in connection with all the murders and crimes that took place while you were at Omarska. Tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a witness? Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does that strike you as strange if you are reporting it, because either you found a body or you saw someone hurt? If you're in the chain of information, are you telling us, all of us as professional persons, that you would not be interviewed by an investigating officer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me as if I had thousands of reports about thousands of dead. I had no information about a single dead. Information, no information. I may have had some observations, and I don't want to mix the two together, personal observations. But if we're talking about information, the only information I had was that there were people who had been beaten up and people with injuries. I never received any information about dead people, except for seeing three or four bodies. I don't wish to conceal that; I hope I'm not giving you that impression. I did see four or five dead people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about your comment, "You're asking me as if I had thousands of reports about thousands of dead." I am indeed asking you exactly that question, and I want to ask you if this was the same question that was asked at your interview. On page 5 of the Bennett interview, page 5 of the interview, where the interviewer asks you, "Do you think that what has been written in books and various articles, namely that between 2.000 and 3.000 people were killed in those camps, is true?" Your answer, "I think it is not. I think that such a figure is out of the question. That it would have been impossible to carry out something like that because I really spent quite a lot of time there. And I do not believe that such things could have happened while I was away." MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a few moments ago Mr. Kvocka denied that he ever gave an interview to Mr. Chris Bennett.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the response, Mr. Kvocka can say, "I didn't say that." It is a question that will be put to him. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was not the point of my objection. I just wanted to object to the wording of Ms. Somers who said, "You told Chris Bennett," and Kvocka has said that he didn't say anything to Chris Bennett. That is all I'm objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Simic, Mr. Kvocka will easily reply, "I didn't say that." So Ms. Susan Somers, put your question to the witness, "Did you say that," and then read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Shall I reread the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay, no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interview to which we are referring has a passage in which there is a question, "Do you think that what has been written in books and various articles, namely that between 2.000 and 3.000 people were killed in those camps, is true?" Your answer, "I think it is not. I think that such a figure is out of the question. That it would have been impossible to carry out something like that because I really spent quite a lot of time there. And I do not believe that such things could have happened while I was away." Are you suggesting that things did not happen at night? Are you suggesting that things did not happen while you were not physically present, albeit on shift? What are you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this confirms everything I have said, only depends on the context you look at it in. I was telling you what could have happened in my presence, but not present in the camp, present at my workplace and what could have happened if I was present among the people. And that is what I told him. Something may have happened when I left 20 days after the camp. According to the books, everyone was killed in those camps. So this is a hypothetical conversation. He says that he's reading in books that so many people were killed. My response is, maybe they were all killed. I'm telling you about what I saw, what I heard, and what I actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on, you were asked, "Do you have any idea of the possible number of people that were killed?" Your words, "No. I never gave that any thought. I know that I personally did not witness any killings." Is this where you cut off your responsibility in your mind, Mr. Kvocka, that you did not witness any killings? Is this what you're telling this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't discuss the question of responsibility with a journalist because he has no idea about the responsibilities of a policeman. The journalist was asking me about my opinions, and I told him I had no idea about any killings because I had not witnessed any. In those days in Prijedor, I could not tell him about what had happened. I do have my own idea about it. I saw four or five dead bodies, and maybe those two persons that were killed during that incident, and I'm not at all trying to avoid that. I also heard about two deaths from natural causes. I didn't see it; I heard about it. Those are my impressions and I can talk about those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see no evidence in this article that the journalist was asking for your opinions. It seems that the journalist came to your home, I presume, because you had been indicted, and he appears to want to talk about the facts that are alleged in that indictment. Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chris Bennett, if you want to know the whole truth, he wanted to see whether I would resist arrest, and as that was my understanding of his position, I received him nicely and we had a principled discussion. I realise that his task was to prepare me for the arrest, and I wanted to let him know that I would not resist but that I would not voluntarily surrender. I suggested it would be better for me to receive a summons and then I would go to Vienna, The Hague, Belgrade, Banja Luka, no matter where, to be tried. But because of my family situation and the environment I was living in, I could not surrender voluntarily. That was the whole purpose of this interview. He wasn't really interested in what I thought or felt at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in terms of the issue of responsibility, on page 2 of the interview, you are asked: "According to the indictments from The Hague, you are responsible for what took place at Omarska. What do you think about that?" Your answer: "Well, I think that I am not responsible, because I never ordered anyone to do anything --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I am sorry, but in order to avoid objections, I think once we heard from the witness -- once we heard from the witness what he said that this was not an interview, that there were no questions and answers between the journalist and the witness, perhaps admit that as a working hypothesis and say, "This document contains such and such information." Then you can put your questions. Otherwise, we are going to have objections all the time. You said, "The journalist asked you this and you answered that." This was all the subject of an objection. If you continue in this manner, you are risking further objections. Do you understand? So let us adopt the hypothesis that this is a document containing some information, and use that information in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to recategorise that. I just wanted to point out to the Chamber that in the very first paragraph, it does specifically state that "Only three days ago, before he was arrested in Prijedor," that would be on page 1, "Miroslav Kvocka, former warden of the camp in Omarska, gave an interview to our reporter." It is from this language, Your Honour, that I'm taking it. I was not trying to impose any type of categorisation that was not there. Also, it was a taped conversation as well. If the Chamber would like - I just wanted to straighten that point out - I'm happy to say, "In the discussion with ..." That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I do not wish to complicate matters further. But Ms. Somers and myself know that Mr. Chris Bennett is deputy manager for crisis situations and not a reporter of Slobodna Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question that I posed to you, if I can remember that far back, is about responsibility and that, in fact, was what the question was. I started to read to you your answer to the question: "According to the indictments from The Hague, you are responsible for what took place at Omarska. What do you think about that?" And you said, "Well, I think that I am not responsible, because I never ordered anyone to do anything that would be contrary to international conventions and if someone did try something like that in my presence I would prevent it. Such actions sometimes brought even my life into danger, but I nevertheless prevented such things, given the fact that I am a professional policeman and that that is the only thing I know how to do." And then you were asked about some of the examples of how you prevented things. Are you telling us, by virtue of what we've just read, that if you had ordered someone to do something contrary to international conventions, that you would feel yourself to be responsible?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means all kinds of things. First of all, Chris Bennett said, "You are indicted as a commander," or you said, "You were the commander," so it is something that he said. Furthermore, somewhere earlier on, I think, he spoke about -- to the effect, "You have no problems. You are not responsible." He was trying to persuade me to surrender. That's what I wish to underline. He said, "You have some command responsibility. I took down the indictment from the Internet," so on and so forth. But that doesn't matter. I told him that I was not guilty because I hadn't done anything contrary to the Geneva Conventions, considering that the rules which governed my activities were not in violation of the Geneva Conventions. I spoke about that yesterday so I don't wish to take any more time. So as an ordinary policeman, an ordinary policeman may issue some orders but to citizens. When you say "orders," it's a very broad concept. One could prepare a whole study about it. A policeman does issue orders to citizens. "Stop," "Come here," "Switch off your engine," "Get out of your vehicle," these are all orders. There are thousands of orders. But a policeman does not issue an order to another policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went on to discuss areas or examples of how you prevented certain bad things from happening. The instances you gave, you said, "... mainly concerned the attempts of some people from outside to enter the Investigations Centre unauthorised and possibly do something. I prevented some people from entering the Centre." Whom did you prevent from entering the centre? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prevented -- now, the question is where is the borderline which implies entering or not entering the centre. But I did prevent entry into the centre by a person, though that was questionable too because he was wearing a military uniform, he had a military booklet, and he had the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authority to enter. I happen to know that person. He was nicknamed Djordjin. He is a well-known petty criminal from the surroundings of Omarska. He came in a drunken state, armed with a rifle. When I saw him from the window of the office making a noise, I realised that he was not coming in any official capacity. So I went out. I heard the words that he was looking for the hodza, cursing his mother, that he would judge him, and so on. I prevented that person from entering. He did enter the camp, he got close to the administration building, so one could say that he had entered. But I removed him from there anyway. I told Zeljko about this and Zeljko told me that the military police had already taken him over and was investigating things. He had a cocked rifle, and all I had was a pistol on me. But in view of the fact that I knew him as a criminal, I didn't hesitate to intervene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying is that he recognised your authority, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not an issue. I was a policeman and he was a petty criminal. I would come across him frequently. I caught him breaking into a kiosk and stealing three boxes of cigarettes, or breaking into a cafe to steal of bottle of cognac. For him, I'm the Lord Almighty at that moment. He is an ordinary village criminal, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other guards on duty who could have handled this? Why did you take this on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about others. I'm talking about myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about Omarska camp. There were other guards; they were on duty, were they not? Were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you intervene?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt capable of doing it and duty-bound of doing it. Maybe others supported him even. The times were very hard. It was not an ideal, regulated society of law and order. If a chief wants something and you are supposed to prevent it, that is a very, very serious situation and it is very difficult to discuss it in this way, as if everything was ideal, automated, regulated. There were guards there who came from who knows where and they were just told that they would be guards and they wanted bad things to happen rather than preventing bad things. Those were the circumstances I was working in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were more capable or possibly more powerful than the other guards, were you not, than the guards there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to gather all of them and submit us to a test so that we can see what power each one -- each of us had. I did what I thought I was capable of. Maybe there may have been other more capable policemen there than myself. We would really have to be tested and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, would you please move on to another question. The witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about what you did in the course of a day on shift. Describe your average day at Omarska, please, how much time you spent in various locations, your office. Give us from morning till evening.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened only on several days, maybe ten days, that I worked from morning till evening. I didn't make any calculations. Half of my working hours were spent in the office of the duty service. We all know where that office was located and how the duty was organised. So from time to time I would leave that office because I felt, I felt superfluous, so to speak, and also because it was -- I felt better outside. Sometimes Zeljko would give me a specific task to carry out. Once I remembered that he brought some cigarettes and he said, "Kvocka, would you please go and distribute these." When I say "please," I'm only paraphrasing. It was actually an order. He told me to distribute these cigarettes to the guards. And on that occasion I actually stole some cigarettes from that package and gave them to Nusreta Sivac who was begging me for cigarettes every day, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is actually for the guards, but the guards heard that. They knew I had taken away some cigarettes that were supposed to go to them. And also, I would be standing outside in front of the building from time to time that other portion of my working hours that I spent there. I would be near the water taps which are located below the duty service office, looking from the window of that office, near the entrance. There were guards who wanted to have contact with the people over there, who were interested in their duties and wanted to know what was going on. And according to Zeljko's instructions or orders, I would from time to time go to the duty station in Omarska. On three occasions I went to my village in my sector to do some job there. There was a fight in front of a cafe there. There was a robbery of a shop in the village of Jelicka on one occasion, and all those places are within my area of responsibility, so from time to time I would go there to see what was going on. I cannot remember all of the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that while you were on shift, while you were officially assigned to work at Omarska camp, you were out running around to other areas that belonged to the jurisdiction, the pre-wartime jurisdiction, of the Omarska Police Department? Is that what you're telling me, that you left?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of the police station department, that is, of my patrol beat, the villages of Krivicka, Jelicka, Maricka, and Gradina. They are still within that area, which is my patrol sector. That is where I am Chief of Patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4 of the discussion that we were looking at in 3/201, page 4, you were asked, "What actually happened when you tried to calm things down? What did you have in mind?" That relates to another question, but your answer was, "Well, nothing happened. People mainly listened to me while I was there, while I was present. I must tell you that I was present there between 12 and 15 hours every day." Isn't the reality that you spent maybe one or two hours in the office, and ten hours outside the office on the premises of Omarska? Isn't that the reality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not what I can conclude from the text that you have just read. We are speaking of the situation in general here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must say that if I read the text that is in front of me, I have to say that there's no mention of "every" day but "during" the day. Not "every" day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The English translation, Your Honours, that I have, I believe that you have, indicates "every" day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it's "during" the day, that's a long workday, isn't it? Did you not alternate 12-hour shifts with Zeljko Meakic? When he was working his shift, you were not working. One of you was present and the other was not. Was that not your agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's what he was trying to achieve when he was absent, that is, in his absence, that there should be one of us on duty on the shift who would have some kind of police experience and knowledge which he would use to prevent such things. And you heard from your own witnesses that Zeljko was there all the time, that he was, that he was -- he would sleep there as well; however, that from time to time, he would absent himself from the camp. During those periods of time, he wanted me to be there and to establish a shift like that there, because he trusted me. He believed that I would inform him of everything, that I would also intervene in cases of trouble, if I see that. So for those reasons, the situation was as it was. And I think that there was a case or two when I spent 15 days -- 15 hours there; however, it was not every day. And this is the way you should read this text. There was a day or two when I spent there 15 days [as interpreted], for example. On the first day I spent there 20 days [as interpreted] because Zeljko went to Prijedor to get instructions and orders and to be briefed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, on the first day you spent 20 hours not 20 days, on the transcript. You never spent 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, about 20 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think we have a problem here. Mr. Kvocka, you have to speak slowly. Everything that we say in respect of other witnesses applies to you as well, because what we can read here in the English transcript is the following [In English]: "There was a day or two when I spent there 15 days." It is not possible to spend 15 days in one day, so we know that's hours. But it's logical, we know immediately that it's hours. So if we are going to interrupt constantly, we don't receive the order. [Interpretation] So Mr. Kvocka, I have to ask you once again to speak slowly so that your words can be adequately entered into the record, and in that way we can avoid problems, unless it's intentional. In that case, there's nothing I can do about it. Mr. Simic, do you have any other objections? I see that you're still on your feet. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're quite right as regards the speed with which Mr. Kvocka is speaking. However, we have to correct what Judge Riad has brought up. What we read in the transcript is the following, that on the first day he spent there 20 days. However, he wanted to say that on that first occasion, he worked two days in a row. That is what I wanted to be entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, could you please clarify the issue; and also, the same applies to you, would you also slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise for my speed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was about the number of hours per day you spent, and I had somewhere back on the transcript asked you if the reality wasn't that you spent one or two hours in the office and the rest of a 12-hour day going around the premises of Omarska camp. And then you gave an answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that approximately half of that time of my shift would be spent in the office, and the other half somewhere outside. So that would be more than one hour or two. Usually during my day shift, and when I say "usually," I say I would usually spend eight, ten, maybe 12 hours there, if I was working full time, which was not very often, from morning till evening. That happened maybe on two or three occasions. During that time, I would probably spend five or six hours in the office and then five or six hours outside the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and Mr. Meakic did not have an agreement whereby one of you would be there for a 12-hour shift and the other would be there for the other 12-hour shift? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I could not have an agreement with Meakic. I could only be ordered to do something by Meakic. I guess you can say that we can't -- we had an agreement, for example, when Meakic told me, "Kvocka, we had an agreement yesterday and you didn't do it," but actually, it was not an agreement. It was an order. It was just the way we spoke. It was a kind of jargon that we used. We used the word "agree." Second, I told you that my impression was that it was his desire to organise things in his absence; that is, when he was absent for a couple of hours, that I should be there. So the schedule would be sort of disrupted. There was a schedule which was in place in principle, but then it would also change according to the situation. Sometimes my shift would be until 10.00, and then he would come and tell me, "Now you are free, you can go, and come back tomorrow around noon." But, you know, the way we speak about these shifts, one would get an impression that I worked there for ten years. I only worked ten or 15 shifts, maybe 20. It's not important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would please look at --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would kindly look at the record of interview between yourself and Investigator Reid which is 3/203.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The English page, Your Honours, is 52, and the Serbo-Croat page would be 57. Again, in English 52, and Serbo-Croat 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 52, you're discussing with Investigator Reid rotation of shifts, and you gave the hours, and then Investigator Reid asks you, or says, "Okay, that's fine. But it was 12 hours in length. And did you work the opposite shift to Mr. Meakic?" Your words, "Yes, one could say that with respect to his order that he would not be there when I was not there, and I would be there when he was not." Again, turning to page 59, which is in Serbo-Croat 64. On page 59 English, looking a little bit below the middle of the page, if it's on the ELMO, where Reid asks you about a concern for yourself and Meakic, et cetera, and you said, "I had no concern there. I just felt it wasn't my business." Then Reid asks you about shifts. "Okay. So now, you've arrived for work or whatever shift it is, the 12-hour shift, can I just try and get some idea of what the structure was as far as the police was concerned? Either yourself, or Mr. Meakic is there, is there or was there somebody below you or Mr. Meakic and above the other police guards, for instance, a shift leader?" This is the second reference to shifts. Which is it, what you're telling us today or what you told Investigator Reid? Which shifts did you work? How many hours a day did you put in? Please tell us. Or is it what you told the person who was involved in the discussion at your home?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all the same, as far as I can see. I always said the same thing. I told you that Zeljko, whenever he was absent for a couple of hours, that he always wanted -- I mean we worked together. We did not have very strict shifts of 12, 24, 48 hours. I don't know what the system would have been. I was there on my shift. If, for example, today the plan was that I would be working for 12 hours, then I would also be off duty for 24 hours after that. However, sometimes what happened would be the following: Zeljko and I were there for 12 hours. Then he would tell me I'm going to continue for several hours more because he had some job to do, or sometimes he would say, "I'm going to leave now and you continue your shift for several hours more, and then you will compensate for that time tomorrow." There is a schedule that is a preset schedule, but there are also -- it was also possible to deviate from the schedule. It is one and the same thing that I told the investigator here, the journalist Chris Bennett, and you. It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. You were asked on page 59 as well about whether or not there were people between -- let me repeat it. The question that Reid asked you was: "... either yourself, or Mr. Meakic is there, is there or was there somebody below you or Mr. Meakic and above the other police guards, for instance, a shift leader?" Your answer: "I know the term. I think that Meakic appointed three people to be shift leaders." Question: "Do you know who those three people were?"

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Do not go on because that's not what it states here. I said I think that he appointed three people to act on behalf of the shift and not to be shift leaders. That is at least what I can read here in my text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question: REID: Do you know who those three people were? KVOCKA: Yes. REID: Who were they? KVOCKA: Milojica Kos, Momcilo Gruban, and Mladjo Radic. REID: Did they have nicknames, those three people? KVOCKA: Milojica Kos was called Krle, Momcilo Gruban was called Ckalja, and Mladjo Radic was called Krkan. Did you have any part in the selection of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in the selection of these people. However, two or three days later, Zeljko told me that certain changes had taken place in the meantime, that the larger number of detainees was expected and that he had to reorganise our work. So far we had been working in 12-hour shifts. Those three first days were actually terrible when it comes to shifts. There were no shifts, properly speaking. He said at that point that he had to organise three shifts at least in order to provide security to such a large number of people, that that was what he had to do. He said that he needed to set up a duty service and that he needed people for this duty service who can use the telephone and radio communications, and that he needed people whom he could trust and people who would inform him about everything that was going on, who would not hide anything from him. He said, "Mladjo Radic is an experienced policeman. He's okay." Then he went on and he said, "Momcilo Gruban is an old reserve policeman, highly respected by his colleagues, so he will be okay too." And then he said, "I don't know about this Milojica guy. He's a new one but he seems to be very nice, very calm and reliable." That is what Zeljko told me. Then I said, "Well, then, why not take him as well? You're free to take him on if that is the kind of impression and conviction you have about him." He mentioned several other names as well. Bob Reid continues with his questions in the interview. Rajko Marmat, Mico Hrvacanin, Stole Vuleta were also considered. Those were all men from the reserve -- special duty service members. There was a need for a larger number of duty officers within this overall security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think we have to make a break at this point. I wanted to finish this area but it doesn't seem to be possible at this point. A half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. So, Ms. Susan Somers, let us continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, having settled on some shifts, can you please describe the hours of the first shift, or generally give the hours of the shifts, if you would do that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, 12 hours you were on duty and 24 hours you were off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when would the 12-hour shifts start, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, 7.00 or 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at your page -- our page 52 in English, and I think that the B/C/S edition was -- let me see, it was page 58 in B/C/S. At the bottom of page 52, the discussion between you and Investigator Reid was: REID: What was the duration of those shifts? KVOCKA: Twelve hours. REID: Did you rotate shifts like you'd work say, from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m. one day, and then on another occasion, 7.00 p.m. to 7.00 a.m.? KVOCKA: Yes. First shift, from 7.00 in the morning till 7.00 in the evening and then from 7.00 in the evening till 7.00 in the morning. But I don't know whether the shifts started at 6.00 or 7.00. REID: Okay, that's fine. But it was 12 hours in length. And did you work at the opposite shift to Mr. Meakic? We've discussed that. How often would a person have an evening shift? Would a person have it two days in a row? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean entire shifts?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. How many times would you work, for example, an evening shift in a row, 12-hour evening shift or a day shift? What was the normal pattern of shifts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it was impossible to work two nights in a row, so if we're doing the day shift today, then the next day we would work the night shift, in the evening. And then the day after that, we would do the day shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that did not apply to you, did it? You did not work night shifts generally, or did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I worked four or five night shifts while I was in the investigation centre, something like that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in general, you had the day shift; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe twice as many day shifts, and that's all. Maybe even fewer. Maybe an equal number. I don't know exactly. I can't add it up now in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were discussing the shift commander selection process. Why was it that Meakic asked you for your input on these commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not a selection of shift leaders. It was a selection of workers to the duty service. No one said that they were shift leaders, nor can Zeljko appoint shift leaders. It is quite a different thing that people called it, loosely speaking, using various terms. I was referred to as a director. When I removed that person from the camp, then people who were nearby applauded and said "Bravo, director." So in some people's minds, I may have been a director. But Zeljko could not appoint shift leaders, nor did anybody say that. I said in this interview with Mr. Reid that that term was also used, not only referring to these three men, but to some others as well. And my input, to come back to your question, was that he thought that as I was older and more experienced as a policeman than Zeljko Meakic, I know people better. I know citizens better. I had spent more time on guard duty with some people. I was on guard duty for three shifts to the side of the administration building, between the entrance and the administration building. These were eight-hour shifts. I don't know why they were shorter shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much older are you than Meakic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already had some ten years of service when he joined the service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we became sector leaders, I think, simultaneously. He may have become that before me, a year before or a year after me. It's hard to remember. But it could be said that we both became sector leaders roughly at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the position of sector leader, did his career take off faster than your career? What was your perception?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no promotion from the position of sector leader, and if we look at him, one could say that he did move up because in March or April, he became commander of the department, if that can be considered a promotion. Actually, it is, yes. After all, it is a step up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's March and April of 1992, Mr. Kvocka? 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to the shift leaders, the term of which you did agree with Mr. Reid was a correct term, please tell us exactly when you first met Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Milojica a long time before the war for the first time, and then I wouldn't see him for a period of time, and then I would see him again. The last few years prior to the war he was a waiter in a catering establishment near the police station where we often went to have coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often would you say you saw Mr. Kos before his taking up his duties at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time. I can't be more precise than that. I would see him three days in a row every day, and then for a month I wouldn't see him at all, and that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Outside that catering establishment we were never in the same company, outside this facility where he was working as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you frequent the restaurant where he was working as a waiter personally, or did your colleagues in the police department frequent it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several colleagues frequented it. It is a restaurant nearby. You just cross over a meadow - and one could call it a park now - 50 metres across a meadow and you reach the establishment. The owner of this restaurant was a lady, a rather good-looking lady. Maybe that was an added attraction. The policemen like to have a cup of coffee in her presence, in her company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was it, if he shared this with you, that Mr. Meakic thought about Mr. Kos that made him, I believe your words were, reliable?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he said that he couldn't make up his mind who should -- he should put in the duty service, then he said, "I don't know this young man very well, but he seems to be a highly reliable and quiet and controlled young man. Perhaps I could put him in the duty service, because I believe he will pass on any information to me and tell me frankly if somebody didn't come to work," because that is an obligation of the duty officer, to record people coming to work. If he gets information about an incident, that he will not cover it up, that he would find Zeljko and inform him about it so that steps could be taken; that if Zeljko was not present, that he would call the duty service in Prijedor which would take over. And it was in that sense that a person had to be reliable, who would not keep quiet about something and who would not delay action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Meakic indicate how well he personally knew Kos, bearing in mind the character reference you've just given us about Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he knew him almost as well as I did during the years that we would meet there for a cup of coffee or in passing in Omarska. I know Kos superficially from his childhood days, that's the only difference perhaps. So he was just hesitating. He knew more or less as much about Kos as I did. He hesitated probably because he was new. That was my impression; I may not be right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to page 71 of the record of interview with Investigator Reid, which would be, let me see, pages 76 and 77 in the Serbo-Croat edition, version, looking in the upper half of the page going toward the middle, Investigator Reid is asking some questions about, "Can you indicate the rooms that the women slept in?" And your response is, "In these two." You were obviously pointing to some diagram or perhaps a model. "I'm indicating B11 and B10." Reid says, "Thank you. And you stated yesterday that the shift leaders, Mr. Kos, Mr. Gruban, and Mr. Radic used this area on the first floor as well. Can you indicate what room they used?" Your answer is, was, "They used B5, the same room as ...." And Reid says, "That's the same room that yourself and Mr. Meakic used?" Your words, "Yes, it's the same one." Were you frequently or infrequently in the same room with Mr. Radic, Mr. Kos, and Mr. Gruban, or any combination of them, while they were on shift?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would frequently be with some of them. And Bob Reid says here that I said they were shift leaders. I never said that they were shift leaders. I tried to clear that up a moment ago. I said that this term was used for some people, and they were among them, but more in the sense chief, boss, or director. As I was saying a moment ago, if you do a good deed, a detainee would say, "Thank you, director." So that was a manner of speaking, the use of these terms. I never told Mr. Bob Reid that they were shift leaders. I think that was quite clear a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your relationship with Mr. Kos, which you have described as superficial, did you feel that that superficial relationship was significant enough or had enough trust for you to ask Mr. Kos to look after your brothers-in-law in the "glass house" after you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would always ask Mr. Kos to do that, but also many others, but not all of them. I am speaking in general terms referring to policemen in general. I would ask Radic or Gruban, and they knew, in view of our relationships as colleagues. But Gruban, as far as I remember, happened to be there when I brought them back, so I addressed him. As for the others, that was implied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On pages 88 and 89 of your interview with Investigator Reid, that would be in Serbo-Croat -- excuse me, 88 and 89 would be 94 and 95. That's 94 and 95. Looking in the bottom half in the English of page 88, there's a discussion that is about a glassed-in area known as the "glass house," and Reid asks you, "How did you know that your brothers-in-law were placed into the glass house after you left the camp?" Your words, "I, I was there when they put them there." Reid, "Okay. And who arranged for them to go into the glass house?" Your words, "One of the guards but I drove them to the building." Reid, "And did you ask, did you ask for them to be put into the glass house?" Your words, "I, I don't know but I told, I don't know what I said exactly but I told Momcilo Gruban, nicknamed Ckalja, to look after them and also to Milojica Kos. Or I might have told Gruban to ask Kos to look after them. Anyway, I knew already that I was leaving the centre so I just asked them to look after them. And we'd know what that means." Reid, "Why the glass house?" Your words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Yes, Mr. Nikolic. No? No objection? I'm sorry for the interruption. Please continue, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reid, "Why the glass house?" Your words, "I had the impression that this was the safest room and the one where, with the best conditions." Did Kos and Gruban look after your brothers-in-law to your satisfaction so that they were not harmed? What was your assessment of the care they gave them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confident that they did as much as they could. However, you heard the testimony of my brother-in-law and the problems with Zeljko Savic, who took advantage of every occasion to provoke them and mistreat them. I don't know all the things that he did to them. Apparently, my brother-in-law doesn't want to tell me everything either. So Kos, Ckalja, Dzigi, maybe Radic, whatever they could do to help was to give them some food, to pass on to them what I was sending them. And if they were brave (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we enter private session for just one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is better. Otherwise, we risk repeating the name. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
