utterances.text: Looking at the discussion between you and a journalist, which is 3/201 which we've referred to today, the English version, page 5, or perhaps bottom of page 4 and then going on to page 5 -- I'm sorry, I don't know the B/C/S page. It's a discussion about your wife's three brothers. So if that would help you find it, Mr. Kvocka, it's talking about your brothers-in-law. At the very bottom of English page 4, you and the interviewer are discussing your brothers-in-law and questions about their stay or lack of stay in Omarska. You do go into mentioning:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to have members of your family or your wife's family who were in Omarska released?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain that to you. I did not try to have them released. For they also had been brought to the Investigations Centre and I thought that if they were guilty of anything in connection with the organising of the attack on the Serbian authorities in Prijedor, they should undergo the procedure, but for the sake of providing for their security when I was absent I put them up with my parents near the camp, the Investigations Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did you have accommodated in their house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife's three brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were being processed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been brought in with the others but I took them away from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were with my parents for about a month and when I left the Investigations Centre I returned them to the Centre again and asked some of my friends to keep an eye on them and that nothing stupid should happen to them. These same friends would be Kos, Gruban, and the other names you mentioned? These are your friends that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some others. I didn't have any particular ones in mind. I considered all of those who respected me as a policeman to be my friends. I'm not talking about any kind of special friendship. Of course some were closer than others. Some had greater trust in my ability as a policeman; others ignored me. So, of course, those who ignored me and swore at me behind my back, I certainly wouldn't address them for any such assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, you didn't use the term "colleagues," "associates," you used the term "friends." Is that what you meant, "friends"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, normally. If you're talking about the name which we won't mention now, he was a friend before he became a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about Kos. He was a friend, from what you have just written -- I'm sorry, what I've read to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the police service, when you have six employees in a remote village, all the policemen automatically are friends. That is the meaning behind it all. I never had any conflict or any incidents among those policemen. They are men who rely on one another, who have to watch each other's back in the case of any intervention. That already becomes friendship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you just specify, when you said, speaking of confining them to your friends, "so that nothing stupid would happen to them," the word stupid doesn't seem very clear to me. Can you just tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the overall situation in the investigations centre, and around it on a broader scale, it was possible to imagine something stupid happening to anyone. He could be beaten; he may even perhaps get killed. Especially in their case, in view of the fact that I was already despised even among some of the guards and a section of the population, something could have intentionally happened to them. They could have been mistreated, humiliated, to put it mildly. He could perhaps -- they could perhaps even get killed. But, anyway, we've heard testimony here that they were threatened, or one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at English page 53 of your interview with Investigator Reid, and that would be page 58 of the Serbo-Croat edition, there is a discussion or question and answer section between you and Reid about what would happen when Zeljko Meakic was not there. I wanted to ask you about how things actually happened when he was not there. Reid asks you -- well, at the top of the page, Reid says to you, "So it would be a case that Mr. Meakic, for instance, as an example, would work from 6.00 a.m. or 7.00 a.m. in the morning, to 6.00 p.m. or 7.00 p.m. in the night, and then you would come on at 6.00 p.m. or 7.00 p.m. and then work through till the next morning?" You respond, "Yes, although it does not necessarily mean that this was always the case." Reid, "No, but generally that was the way it was to work?" You answered, "Yes." Reid, "Now, I've discussed this with you before but I'm just not clear. When Mr. Meakic was not in the camp, who was in control of the police security?" Your answer, "It's difficult for me to explain. In a certain sense, and that was the general impression, that I was. I would say that part of the policemen, the newly recruited reserve policemen thought that way. That's it." Reid asks you, "But in your mind, when you were there without Mr. Meakic, say working from 6.00 p.m. or 7.00 p.m. at night to 6.00 a.m. or 7.00 a.m. the next morning, who in your mind was in charge of the interrogation centre as far as the police and the security were concerned?" Your words, "It was considered that that was me. And Zeljko told me, Zeljko ordered me to look after the things that I mentioned before." Reid asks you, "And did you see as your role when you were, as you say, the person in charge when he was away, as running the interrogation centre the same way as he would run it, with the same authority that he had?" Your answer, "I'm not sure how to answer this question, it's not quite clear. In a certain sense, I would look as if I were in charge. I did not have a place like all the other guards. I had Zeljko's order and the request to help him, help the people who did not know their job." Reid, "Would you agree with me, though, that there must be somebody in charge when the commander is not there?" Your words, "Generally, yes." Reid, "Would you see that person as being you?" You answer, "I personally don't. I was never a commander in my life." Reid, "Then who, then see the problem is, if that's what you were thinking, then what occurred was that there was nobody responsible for the running of the interrogation centre?" Your words, "That's possible." Reid, "Okay. You said earlier that the guards, or the police officers would have seen you as the person in charge when Mr. Meakic wasn't there?" Your word, "Yes." Reid, "Do you believe that the prisoners would also have seen you in that light as well?" Your answer, "Yes, they could get that impression." You have heard months of testimony from various people who have said just that. Do you recall, and I will be very specific, the testimony of Witness J, Witness J, whom you knew for a long time? I am looking, for reference for the record, I'm looking at the transcript of Witness J, open session, page 4742.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Miroslav Kvocka, what role did he play in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Kvocka was Zeljko Meakic's deputy, that is to say, the Deputy Commander of the Omarska camp. Moving down a little bit, "Q What do you mean that the guards talked about it?" I'm sorry let me move up a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to know about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was no secret. People talked about it. The guards talked about it, and you could tell by his conduct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, what do you mean that the guards talked about it? What would you hear the guards say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would say, "I have to ask the deputy. I'm going to see the deputy. I'm going to see Kvocka," that kind of thing. And then they move down a little bit, and Witness J is asked by the Prosecution:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear Kvocka issuing instructions to the guards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He acted like a superior and would tell the guards where to go. He would say, "Go to that section." He would give them their schedule. They liked him, always listened to the orders or instructions he gave them. I never heard anybody refuse to act upon his word. The witness was asked, "Did you have occasion to observe how the guards treated Miroslav Kvocka?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I really do not wish to interfere with your line of questioning, but I have to intervene at this point. Do you really need to read and repeat everything that is already in the record in order to ask your question? You can see the transcript, that we have a number of questions and answers, and we will no longer know who they can be attributed to, whether it was before or after. It's really up to you. We decided that you can do, of course, as you please with the time that is allotted to you, but I must draw your attention to the fact that you repeat many things. Maybe it would have been enough to mention the page of the transcript that you wish to quote; otherwise, we will be making too many repetitions and too many re-readings of the transcript, but, of course, you can do as you please. At least, I think that it would be good if you have to quote the transcript, then you -- it would be good if you can just tell us for the record that it's a quote, and then unquote. Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, I really do not understand the purpose of the quoting of the testimony of a witness and then for this witness to be asked to comment upon them. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to take into account that our memory is a bit restricted and limited, and perhaps it is better to provide us with the relevant piece of information, and then to ask your question, that is to say, that you can perhaps give us small portions of the text that you want to quote so that we can remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate very much your comments. And the purpose was because it was really quite a long -- it was September 5th of 2000, it was a while back. And the issue was to tie in these particular comments to what was just read from the record of interview, and because of the several months that have gone by and the number of witnesses this Chamber has listened to, it was effectively to make sure that what was said by the witness himself was borne out very much by the witness whose testimony I just quoted. So, yes. And I do appreciate -- I'm sensitive to the time issue as well. I want to make sure that the Chamber has the page numbers and that certainly my learned counsel opposite also are aware of where to look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague has just confirmed something that I have recognised as a pattern. The purpose was not laying foundation for a question but to analyse the words of a witness which was part of the evidence. This is simply a cross-examination of a witness who is supposed to talk about the facts that he's familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, we can understand that. We can conclude that. It was perhaps not necessary for you to say that. I think that Ms. Somers is perfectly aware of that. Ms. Somers, will you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking back at page -- let me see, now. I may have lost my train. Oh, yes, we were at the top of page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I simply have to intervene. Is Ms. Somers, once she has quoted the testimony of Mr. Kvocka and the testimony of Witness J, is she going to ask Mr. Kvocka to explain this to her? Is that the purpose, Mr. Kvocka's explanation? Is he going to explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, do you not have a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please ask your question. Mr. Kvocka has been waiting for your question, and he is getting impatient because he's simply not getting the opportunity to give you an answer. Would you please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness for making him wait so long. Mr. Kvocka, what you have just heard Witness J say about you is - very, very much as we've just read - consistent with what you had said about yourself. Did you get the impression that most of the people whom you met were getting the impression that you were in charge? I'm only asking you, do you think they were getting the impression that you were in charge when Meakic wasn't there. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection again. I apologise, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I have to tell you that you are acting in a paternalistic manner. You're trying to protect your witness. He has a very special status here at this point. He doesn't need your protection. Please, let Mr. Kvocka testify; otherwise, Mr. Simic, your frequent objections will be beside the point, and I will have to proceed in a different manner. I really do not wish to threaten you in any way. I am not here to do that, but there are provisions - I'm not going to quote them - in our rules and regulations which concern the conduct of the proceedings, in order for the proceedings to be conducted in a smooth way, in order for witnesses to be able to testify in an adequate manner. So, please, Mr. Simic, try to restrain yourself. Ms. Somers, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in fairness to you, I'll repeat the question. It was a bit of a gap. I asked you -- or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to us, what was the impression you got?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You skipped approximately 20 pages from the interview with Bob Reid where I talked to him about the impressions and what kind of job I was doing and what kind of instructions I was getting from Zeljko Meakic, when he came in the morning and when he told me that I would go to see the policemen till 3.00 in the afternoon and tell them about their duties and tasks. So I would be doing that on that day. If he told me to distribute cigarettes to the policemen on that, I did, then I would distribute cigarettes on that day. I cannot remember all of the instructions that he gave me, but most of the things concerned the newcomers, the newly-arriving policemen and what kind of things needed to be explained to them. Because I already told you, we were not, properly speaking, alternating with each other. Sometimes we would be together, and sometimes he would stay later or I would stay later. He would simply tell me to go to see the policemen, to tell them this or that, to tell them that they should not have contact with the detainees. Or, for example, he told me that he had been on that day with Simo Drljaca, and that he told me that policemen should not be talking with the detainees. So those were the kinds of things that I did, plus some other things that I did. And I know it is very hard for me to talk about all the things that I did in order to help the people there. This is already common knowledge, and it has been stated by your witnesses as well. So that's what I can say as regards the impressions. So those were the impressions that people had. But they can only comment on these impressions themselves. Witness J spoke about her impressions, and she never said at any occasion that I had ordered anything. She only said that it seemed that I was ordering things. I said that -- she said that I would be talking to policemen, but she didn't say that I had ordered something to that effect. She has the perfect right to make her own conclusions from her own impressions. I could go on about this as much as you want me to, but I am also mindful of your time. I don't wish to be speaking all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like you to try to help us understand is, was it from the distribution of cigarettes at the request or on the order of Meakic that gave so many people the impression that you were in charge, or -- it's been repeated that prisoners got the impression, guards got the impression. What do you think it was in your conduct that would have given that impression? Not cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that was that, my overall conduct, my overall behaviour which gave rise to various kinds of impressions. One gentleman stated here that I was like a God Almighty to him at this moment, though at this point I can say that he invented the fact that I had written a note because there were no notes whatsoever. I am not excluding the possibility for a guard who wore a police uniform for the first time to see me whom he knew as a policeman from his village, and then asking me, "This particular detainee would like to go somewhere, can I let him go?" So in that case, I could tell him, "Yes, you can do that," but there was no talk whatsoever about any notes. If you give a piece of bread to someone, then the person whom you gave this bread would say, "Thank you, chief, thank you, boss." And I think that that particular person said at that moment that I was the God Almighty for him at that moment. So these are the kinds of impressions that I'm talking about. Impressions were based on certain acts which we can discuss here, whether they're negative or positive. I cannot find any negative act that I may have done, at least I haven't been able to see it so far. And I think that my mistake was that I was a bit, perhaps, too prominent in respect of others in that sense. You're maybe trying to misinterpret it, but it is up to Their Honours to decide upon that. I wasn't trying to hide myself and to perform my duties in secret, in absence of everyone. I would bring a car full of parcels, and I would divide -- distribute those parcels in the centre of the compound. If anyone was looking at that from the side, then perhaps he could conclude that I was the most powerful person over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to get physically rough with your guards? Did you ever have to get bullyish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, concerning the record. We do not have a sentence, "While others were bringing parcels and hiding their parcels under their arm, and I was doing that publicly and I think that it was a honourable thing to do."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that something was said. I would like to ask the interpreters whether they are really interpreting what the witness is saying or not? Mr. Simic, I think I already discussed the issue with you. What was the sentence that you heard and that the interpreters failed to interpret? I think that you said the witness has said something which has not been entered in the record. Is that what you're saying? THE INTERPRETERS: Microphone, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, upon a question asked by Ms. Somers speaking about the impression, Mr. Kvocka said, and I paraphrased, something to the effect that he publicly brought a car full of parcels and publicly distributed them; whereas others were doing that, hiding a sandwich, for example, under their arm and giving it to the prisoners in secret. So in such a situation, I could have seemed to appear different from others to a person who was observing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, they would add the sentence, something to the effect, "This is the most powerful man that we have known so far." I know some people from the compound, from the pista, who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But were there any other people who were doing the same thing as you did but in secret?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many of the guards, as one witness said the other day, had a Muslim they knew, or every Muslim had a Serb that he knew, so one could notice that. But somehow they were trying to hide this from each other, in view of the overall atmosphere. I do not wish to describe it in detail because we all know what kind of atmosphere it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, can I ask you to speak slowly, to slow down, because the interpreters cannot interpret everything that you say. Counsel can understand what you are saying. Because if you continue to speak fast, we will be faced with the question, "Is that really what Mr. Kvocka said or not? Did he say something else?" Mr. Kvocka, speak more slowly, please, because we've already given you the sign to that effect several times. So maybe it is up to you yourself to think of the work we have to do. I will not allow further objections by Mr. Simic to say, "He said this and it's not in the transcript." So it's up to you. Speak slowly and then the interpreters will be able to interpret everything that you say. If not, it is not fair, in my opinion. It is not up to your counsel to testify instead of you. I know you're a brave man and that you're saying what you're saying, I know that. But so as to have no doubt about it, we must avoid such a situation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, excuse me, just to understand something which was said. You said that you could come with a carful of sandwiches, whereas others would hide them because the others were afraid. You were not afraid?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that I didn't act in secret. But I was afraid. I didn't act secretly because I felt I was doing the right thing. Others would bring a sandwich under their arm, a small sandwich. I'm sure you've heard testimony about it and I feel embarrassed to keep repeating these things, but you have heard that I would bring a carful of parcels. This is something quite conspicuous. And everyone, maybe not quite everyone, but people did give things to others in secret, hiding a sandwich or a small bag of something. So that is the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you thought you would get away with it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about consequences. True to my own life and my police career, I continued to act in that way. I was aware somewhere in the back of my mind that this was dangerous, that there was an imaginary danger or a danger which could be discerned, in view of the circumstances. That nationalist tensions were running high, I was aware of that. But in my own mind, when I juxtapose that to what I was doing, that is, what I was doing and what could happen, then my decision to act in that way gained sway because I wasn't violating any written rules. The fact that I was acting against somebody's ideas was not a good enough reason for me not to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kvocka. I must say that you have made an effort to speak more slowly, and so when you hurry up again, I will let you know by waving my hand. Please continue, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're a long way from my question, but just as part of this question, you've indicated you never did have any disciplinary action brought against you for any of the generous distributions of the parcels that you engaged in, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, no. Officially, according to how I understand things, that was not possible, because it was not in violation of any rules that were in force in those days. It was not prohibited to socialise with a Muslim or to assist a Muslim, according to the law. But if in somebody's heads that was prohibited, they couldn't institute any official disciplinary proceedings, because where would that lead? What would they refer to? What law would they refer to? You see, in somebody's heads, people could condemn me and reject me and ignore me and sidestep me for various reasons. Not just the parcels. The parcels are a minor thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back a little bit. I had asked you if you were perceived by your guards as a bully, a person who was physically aggressive with them. Was there ever an incident that you can recall where you had to get aggressive with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think there wasn't any incident with a guard in which I was aggressive. There was no need. These were all guards from the surrounding villages who knew me and knew my reputation as a policeman. If - if, and again I'm speaking hypothetically - if somebody had in his mind the intention of beating up somebody and if he knew that I would see that, he would give that up, his intention, because he would know that I would intervene. I worked for 20 years in the villages from which the guards came and they knew how I acted in the village when they had a fight in front of a cafe, when they gathered together in the evenings. They knew how I prevented such incidents and brawls. They knew that in a bar, if somebody was mistreating a guest or a waiter, I would always intervene. As a policeman, if I witnessed something and ignored it, pretended that it wasn't happening, I can't remember any such case of my turning my back on such an incident. During my years of service prior to the detention centre, in the detention centre and after that detention centre, and especially in Prijedor -- in fact, I enjoyed taking steps in 1994 in Prijedor. That was the first time I handcuffed somebody, as I mentioned, and this one happened to be a Serb, a Serb extremist, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You drew, from what you're telling us, heavily on your skills with commanding respect. You interacted well with people. Would you assess your interaction ability with people as good?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to give you a yes or no answer to that question. There were some people who, in my impression, fully agreed with my opinion about these things, that people should not be mistreated, that people should not be contacted. Because according to Zeljko's orders, we had been given such instructions, and also information that such contacts were being used for other purposes. So a certain number of people agreed with me in that, but others were against that. That was my impression; that was the feeling I had. The only thing is, either they didn't dare in my presence because they knew I would intervene or for some other reason I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the witnesses who have come here on your behalf, one of them I can think of, spoke of your indignation at the rough handling of a detainee and that you intervened in order to demonstrate the correct handling. I think it was Mr. Brane Bolta who had very high words of praise for your intervention, if you recall. Did you find yourself intervening with the guards who were working at Omarska to show them, generally, the right way to do things, given your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concern about their undertraining and your pride in police work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I intervened whenever I noticed any rough handling. In this particular case, it was my observation, because this was a special group of people who were doing the search. They were the special police, and when you use that term in our system, and I see in other systems and in movies too, when the special police appear, everyone else falls quiet, they no longer exist. So under those circumstances, I had the courage to say that it wasn't a good way to act, and I suffered consequences because of that observation. A man from the special police caught me by the throat and shook me up and said, "What do you mean by grumbling all the time? Tito's time and the time of Tito's police is over," he said to me. But I was such a person that I couldn't keep quiet about it because this happened. I saw it happening, that the search was going on, and there shouldn't have been a search anyway because they were being brought from Prijedor, in a police van, and they had already been searched over there, because they had spent some time in custody. So that search was over. These special policemen just felt like searching them for no real reason and acted roughly. Those were the reasons why I made that observation. The person, I think it was Lukic or maybe Strazivuk, I can't remember exactly which one of the two, one of them was very calm and composed, a very nice man, he was present there on the other side of the police van where I was too, and his comment too was, "What can we do with these wild ones?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your sense of professionalism and training gave you the confidence to intervene and at least indicate what the correct procedure was, the procedure in which you were trained. Is that a fair assessment of the basis for your confidence or one of the bases for your confidence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be put that way. One could say that I am a self-confident policeman. I am confident of what I studied and what I know how to do, and that working for so many years, I had no problems as a result of the way I worked. So I do have a certain degree of self-confidence. But to use that self-confidence against a new special police, a Serb police, when he said that our times and the times of Tito were over, that is something you would have to think twice about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did it because you knew it was right, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced that the least I could do was just to make that observation. It wasn't particularly rough. Nusret Sivac wasn't really hurt at all. It wasn't a drastic incident, but it was humiliating under normal conditions. Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention your concern about this type of handling to Zeljko Meakic? Did you try to address how to prevent this in the future?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were conversations to that effect. There were guards, some guards, I must say - I don't know what each and every one of them had in their mind - but there were some guards who wanted to throw down their rifles and abandon their posts because they couldn't work because of those special policemen. This was true especially at the beginning. Zeljko himself would say, "I don't know what to do." We saw here from the documents what actually happened. He had to -- Simo Drljaca had to intervene to collect information from the staff of the camp; to ask the chief from Banja Luka to contact the staff; that people were out of control; that their own commander could not keep them under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Drljaca support you in what you did?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned Drljaca. He couldn't stand the sight of me. There was no support that I could expect from him. I saw here the document that he sent to Banja Luka. As for the relationship between the two of us, that is quite a different story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't really asking from a personal perspective but as a professional policeman. Your position was supported. You were not reprimanded; you didn't suffer any official consequence. This is what I meant by "support." Having explained that to you, did Drljaca support you in your position and bring about some control there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of information he had. I was not reprimanded, nor should I have been. I acted correctly. All I know is that the special policemen left. If that fits into your question, maybe that is the answer. The special police left. We saw here from the documents that there was correspondence between Drljaca and staff coordinators, as this lady said the other day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they left, in your opinion, did you see that there was more control at least among the ranks? There was not that type of wildness that so made you upset and reactive with the special police.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is obvious. After they left, there wasn't wildness, at least I'm saying what I saw. I didn't see any instances of wildness. I told someone, I don't remember whom and when, that once during the night, from a relative of mine on my wife's side, they seized money, a watch, and rings from Dedo Crnalic. And the commander of the special unit then was somebody called Kokic. I may be wrong with the surname. Lukic, possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to pinpoint a date when the special police left the premises?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two weeks from the beginning, because they came on the 29th in the evening or the 30th in the evening. I'm really not able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of May? Of May?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So on the 14th or the 15th of June they left. The impression they gave was a drastic one. They used armoured vehicles and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your own guards upset about their presence there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard that there were a number of guards who were ready to throw away their rifles, but now when I look back from this time distance, I know that some people would just abandon their work posts. They would come to take up their shifts, and when the duty officers puts a cross indicating that he had come to work - and this is the duty of the duty officer to make a record of that - so what some would do would go out as soon as they got that cross. So that may have been one of the reasons, too. And some people managed to evade things in this way, but I'm saying "some."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see if I can find the reference and ask you a quick question about it. Do you remember discussing some concerns in the camp with Kos and perhaps Gruban? Did you, did you discuss your worries about conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing officially. There were no official conversations between us. But as individuals who would relatively frequently find ourselves in the same shift, we could raise such subjects saying that the conditions were not good and that sort of thing. My understanding of your question leads me to say that I personally was not worried about myself. I was not concerned. There was a witness who said in his statement - he didn't come to testify - that I had lost a lot of weight as compared to what I looked like before the war. I read such statement of one of your witnesses, but he wasn't called to testify. I don't know why. He would have cleared up many other things as well. We wouldn't have to spend so much time about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just take a quick look at your interview with Mr. Reid, on page 60 in the English, and it would be 65 in the Serbo-Croat edition. At the very -- tell me if you have your page. Okay. At the very bottom of the page, Reid is asking you about the conditions in which the prisoners were accommodated in the camp, in the centre, and you said, "I can't remember." But then Reid asked you:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk about the lack of facilities like the toilet facilities that you said had broken down and become blocked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. It's possible that we mentioned these topics. But we couldn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that? Why couldn't you change anything? You say you can't change it, you wouldn't change anything, but Mr. Meakic has expressed concern about the conditions, you've expressed concerns about the conditions, Mr. Radic, Mr. Kos and Mr. Gruban have expressed concern about the conditions, that is, if I could say, the five most senior police officers working at the centre, have expressed concern, and nothing's been done. Turning to the top of 61:

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no possibilities. What could we do? I could bring food from home and that was it. I had no other obligations but humanly I could do nothing more. We couldn't build a building. There was nothing we could do. Can I ask you, you had some equipment there, maintenance equipment, hammers, shovels, hoes, basic equipment that you would have in an industrial compound, did you not; or, at least, the mine company there would have had in its store room some equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a policeman in a police station department. We don't have hammers; we don't have equipment. There may have been all kinds of things, even helicopters in the mine, but I really don't know. There was a manager, so-called manager, who controlled that equipment that you are mentioning, and I do believe that it did exist. I personally didn't see it, but it is to be assumed that in an organisation of that kind, there must be hammers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or any one of the people whose names we just mentioned try to find some equipment, for example, build latrines. Let's go out and dig some trenches so they could be used as extra toilets. Did anybody do that, or try to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any special material anywhere. There was no such material that was easily accessible. There was heavy machinery there. There were no wooden boards, maybe not even shovels. These are large shovels that can move 20 cubic metres at one go. These are big, enormous machines, excavators. So I didn't see anything like that at hand. But I'm telling you, it really wouldn't have been appropriate to interfere in somebody else's responsibilities because there was a manager of the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, we've looked at that order from the 31st of May, 1992, and the last provision, of course, puts the implementation of all the paragraphs in there on Mr. Jankovic who is in your chain of command as a police officer. So the question really is, did anyone try to take any available equipment that would logically, as you suggested, be found in an industrial complex and dig some holes in the ground to use as toilets, to dig holes? Did anybody do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything in that area. This is all speculation. Whether somebody discussed something with Jankovic, the manager Babic or somebody else in another shift, I really don't know. I didn't notice anything being done. I know that there were a certain number of bathrooms. Whether they were sufficient or not, I don't know. They're not sufficient. Most probably in relation to the number of people present, they were certainly inadequate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw that people were not able to bathe. You talked about going near -- I think you used the term water fountains or water something, taps. Did anybody bother to allow some extra time with water running for people to bathe, to wash, to get the lice out of their hair? Was that so difficult to do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not difficult, and I saw that there was a tap with a concrete basin, with actually five or six taps, and the water was running all the time. And whenever I passed by or looked through the window of the duty room, I never noticed it being vacant or free. There was always someone there washing from the waist up or something like that, which doesn't mean to say that I'm saying it was good or sufficient, and it probably wasn't appropriate, because people should be able to bathe normally in a bathroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any women --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, perhaps it's a good time to break for the lunch break. But before we do that, to make things quite clear, I would like to go back to this question of objections by Mr. Simic. I have said that objections should be made when there is a reason for them, a firm reason, which cannot be overcome in any other way. But I always said that there was the possibility for a re-examination to clear up a certain point. The content of your objection regarding other people who were hiding sandwiches is an excellent example of what I'm saying, because in your re-examination you could have later asked Mr. Kvocka, "You said that you brought sandwiches in a car, that everybody could see. Were there other people who brought sandwiches." He would say yes. Question, "How did they bring those sandwiches?" He would say, "Under the arm." There you are. It's quite possible. The rules we have here, as you know, is that one party calls its witnesses. That party examines in chief, the other party cross-examines, and then first party re-examines. We are now in the Defence case. The Defence examines, the Prosecutor cross-examines, and the Defence re-examines. So if every time you need to make an observation to correct something, to draw the attention of the Chamber to something, that mixes up everything, and it is not possible to work in that way. Order, discipline, and we have the rules. So I want to make that quite clear, to use this as an example of what I said. Many of your objections could be dealt with through the re-examination. Let the other party do their work. You all know that you have to do your work, and when you're interrupted, something is upset. If you enjoy being interrupted, then you could say at the beginning, "Interrupt me as much as you like because I enjoyed it," and the other party will find many reasons to do that. But if you don't like that, then respect the other party when it is doing its work. So let me repeat once again; I'm saying this only to make things quite clear. I would not like the hearing time to be transformed into training classes. Mr. Simic, I know that you're a very good lawyer, but you could improve a lot. So now we're going to have lunch for 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I add something? I'm constrained to say something on Mr. Simic's behalf here. I understood that he was not -- that his objection was that Mr. Kvocka had answered the question, had answered the question, but that the translation into English, at least, did not carry his full answer. I think that's very different from a question of whether or not he didn't complete and he wants to finish it someplace else. I think if a witness answers a question, I think -- I agree with you. Everyone should speak slower because it is very hard for the translators, and the translators have a terrible job. I understand that and I sympathise with them fully. But if it happens, that the translation doesn't pick up part of the witness's answer, then I don't think you can ask the lawyer to wait until rebuttal time comes to try to pick -- that's a technical difference. It's not anything about his strategy of objecting. I just want to say that because that's -- it seems to me that's different from the question of whether or not he's objecting to the form of the question or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I quite agree. Maybe now is not the time to continue the discussion. I quite agree with what Judge Wald just said. Those are two different things. But in any event, we also have to trust the interpreters because otherwise, Mr. Simic will not only be the attorney, but also the interpreter. And what I'm saying is, there's no prejudice for the Defence if the Defence says, "I think I heard something like that," and now we can clarify that point. Because otherwise, we have to have a meeting with interpreters to ask them, "Did you hear that? Why didn't you not interpret what the witness said?" And so on. So my question -- my point is, if we trust the interpreters, and I do, I do accept that there may be things that are left out, but that is also the job of the attorney here, to keep note of what was left out. And in the interests of the smooth conduct of the proceedings - this may be a matter of methodology - the smooth conduct of proceedings, it may be preferable to pick it up in the re-examination than to interrupt to say "The witness said this. It was not registered in the transcript." But I'm telling you that my concern is always to maintain what I keep saying to the parties. There are two things which, in my opinion, need to be respected and which are always, but always, nonnegotiable for the rendering of justice: That is the fair treatment of the parties, and the absolute respect for the adversarial principle. So, if there is equality of arms and the other party is always given a chance to respond, then I think that no one, no single person of good faith can say that we have not rendered justice. I'm not saying to Mr. Simic that you cannot make that objection. What we're talking about is the opportuneness of making those objections in the best interests of the smooth running of the proceedings. But I quite agree with what Judge Wald has just said, it is not a question of form, and that is why I think that you can just make a note or Mr. Lukic can do that. You are working in a team. Take note of it, and when the time for re-examination comes, you can pick it up. I am saying this just to maintain a certain degree of order and discipline in our work; otherwise, there will be general confusion which it is very difficult to overcome. So I come back to my 50 minutes for the break. Perhaps our stomachs need comforting, and we will refresh ourselves and come back in 50 minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. So, having had a very useful and fruitful discussion and hopefully a very good lunch, I think that we are now ready to proceed. Ms. Somers, would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in support of one of your witnesses who appeared, you have submitted an affidavit of an individual -- can you hear me okay --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- named Rade Knezevic. Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the comments that is made in the affidavit of Mr. Knezevic - I shall just read it unless the Chamber would like, I can put on the ELMO and have it read from - one of the comments that was made by Mr. Knezevic concerned the use of force as a law enforcement practice in the former Yugoslavia. I wondered if you could assist me in understanding what he may have meant by this. I shall read it, if I may. "While I was working in Omarska, shouting, raised voices, and even moans could sometimes be heard from certain offices while questioning was being conducted. This was because there was a large number of new investigators and reservists who were inexperienced and who lost their tempers easily. I was never inside another investigator's office, however, nor did I see force being used. I have to mention, however, that on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, force was often used in police work during investigations in order to extract confessions and such like." Can you first tell us what position, if any, Rade Knezevic had in Omarska camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an investigator. He was a police inspector and he was an investigator there. I don't know whether that can be considered as a position. That was the kind of job that he was tasked with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that mean that he was a person who carried on the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with his comments that are in the affidavit that I have just read about an acceptable use of force in former Yugoslavia police practices? Is that your opinion as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of force, according to the regulations, is not acceptable, I mean the force itself was not acceptable. However, practice was different. If you're talking about practice, I think that he was, indeed, referring to that aspect of the use of force and I think I can agree with him. During certain investigations, force would be used. I was never, generally speaking, present at any investigation. But it would happen from time to time for a police officer, that is, for all members of the police, to use force. I'm also referring to simple policemen who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. involved on certain minor petty offences, disturbances of law and order and suchlike. It would happen from time to time during such interventions that they overstepped what was appropriate, if, again, we are talking about interventions when it was possible to use force. In their attempts to re-establish law and order, it would happen from time to time that the participants would receive more beatings than usual, if that was the kind of practice that Mr. Knezevic was talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work with him before you saw him at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked in the same building, that is, at the Prijedor Police Station, and I was working in a Prijedor Police Station department. That is, we worked within the same kind of organisation. But he retired several years prior to the war. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he came back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt, Ms. Somers. Mr. Kvocka, as regards this practice that we're discussing right now, was there any difference between persons who had undergone appropriate training in police academies, and other policemen who had not undergone this type of specific formation or training? Was there any difference in your opinion between these two types of officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was a difference between them. There was a very small number of educated policemen, if I can call them that way, at that time; and they knew exactly when to stop, that is, when the reasons for the use of force would cease. So they probably respected those regulations better than some others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka. Please continue, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Knezevic prior to his retirement an active-duty police officer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an active-duty inspector in the homicide department. That is where he worked for a while, I think. Some changes occurred within that department at that time. I think he worked there. People knew him as an inspector. He was a well-known inspector at that time. I don't think he had any unresolved cases. He was well respected as an inspector within that department, that is, the homicide squad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him to employ tactics in extracting confessions that would be considered use of force or excessive use of force during his career?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never heard of such a thing happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to recall any time in your career in any department where you may have worked where excessive force or force was used against an unarmed individual or suspect and resulted in disciplinary action?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against him, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any officer, anyplace that you have worked, are you aware of any disciplinary action being taken against any officer, any investigator, in any of the institutions in which you may have worked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many disciplinary actions during my time of service. As regards specific examples against whom and on what grounds, that would be very hard for me to tell you. There was a number of disciplinary actions that were taken against the people who were members of our police station that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you can remember, you cannot recall right away anyone who was disciplined for using excessive force against a suspect in custody?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember anything specific; that is, I cannot remember against whom such proceedings would have been used. You know, it's a very complex and difficult matter. If a police officer overstepped his duties, that could be considered almost as a criminal offence which then -- which would then mean that that would be within the competence of the investigation section, and that would fall within the responsibilities of the public prosecutor, and no disciplinary action would be taken if excessive force was used. Such things would usually happen during various kinds of intervention, and they were more frequent in -- within the police, the use of excessive force. For example, if you have a fight that's broken out in a cafe, everything would calm down, for example, and then after that, after the situation has calmed down, if a police officer should use -- should continue to react, then that would constitute the use of excessive force. That is, once the situation has calmed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in any of the other camps in the area, Manjaca or Keraterm or Trnopolje, while they were functioning, operational camps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Trnopolje. I was never in Manjaca. I did pass by Trnopolje on several occasions along the road. I'm sorry, by Keraterm. I apologise. I passed by Keraterm along the road on several times. I never went to Manjaca; it's far away. I never had to go there. As regards Trnopolje, I went there only once when I went there to get my brothers-in-law, to get them out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police stations in Prijedor town, how far are they, the police station or stations, located from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us, please, I'm not sure of what you would pass first, but would you have to use the same road of access to Keraterm -- would the road for both be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: If you're coming from the direction of Banja Luka, the Keraterm factory, and that was the name of the factory, is located at the entrance to the town of Prijedor on the right-hand side of the road. If you continue along the same road, you have to take a turn to go into Prijedor town, and the road goes on towards Bosanski Novi. After you've turned towards the centre of the town, you would be on the road leading up to the police station which is located at the very heart of the town, in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the Tukovi reserve or wartime police station from the main police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 3 kilometres, maybe even 4. I don't know. It's difficult for me to be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were discussing yesterday, and I wanted to just get a little clarification, when you indicated that there was a structural change in Omarska's Police Station status at the time of -- well, basically, May of 1992 or at least by May of 1992, whereby it once again became a police station, where Omarska became a police station, we had discussed --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992, no, never. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no changes whatsoever and I never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have discussed this issue. We discussed it yesterday, Mr. Simic. Mr. Kvocka doesn't skip anything. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know he doesn't. However, with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we were overlapping each other so not everything we said is on the record. Please continue, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, I have to say that the purpose of my objection was not the protection of Mr. Kvocka. He is talking about the facts that he is familiar with. It was the matter of protection of myself as his lawyer. If I should accept the pattern that has been adopted by my learned colleague, then I will have to spend three days here and read, I don't know, page 15, line 24 of this or that text. That is what I wanted to avoid. My intention was not to offer any kind of protection of my client. He is here to speak the truth, to talk about the facts he's familiar with. However, I have to draw attention to these kinds of leading questions or, rather, assertions or conclusions which should not be made part of the record. I apologise for my intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers, this concerns what we still see on the screen, but it is about to disappear: [In English] "... when you indicated that there was a structural change in Omarska Police Station ... whereby it once again became a police station." We discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, and I asked the question very simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Put the question but don't state this. It's because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a claim, an allegation. I think that we discussed the issue yesterday. You cannot allege that what was now the police station department in Omarska at one point in time became the police station. That is contested. You cannot claim that; you cannot make such assertions. We are not making closing arguments here. You are still cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was basing my -- the form of my question on what was read from the record of interview between Mr. Reid and Mr. Kvocka from yesterday. But I will gladly rephrase that. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You really have to be aware of that. I've always said you have to ask clear, concrete, and concise questions. If you do that, you will avoid any objections. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the term "wartime police station," particularly referring to Omarska, is that a term with which you were familiar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, from theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to please distribute 3/208.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what you have in front of you is a list, dated the 21st of June, 1992, and it is from an organisational unit which has been called the Wartime Police Station Omarska. Do you recognise some of the names which are on this list? If so, could you just read out one name or two names which you recognise so we can identify it as the same department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know quite a few of them, as far as I can see, but I will have to search my memory. Members of the army unit helping out, I don't know almost anyone here. Then the employees in the RzR. Branko Kecima, I believe he was a driver. Milorad Stakic, as well, he was a driver too with the mine company. Who else? Cedo Vuleta, I know him. He was here the other day. Dragoje Latincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, can you tell us the number next to the name so we can follow you more quickly. It would be easier for us because we are not very familiar with these names. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. From the list where it says "Members of the Army Unit Helping Out," I think I only know number 10, Uros Vuceta, if that is the same person, because it is always possible that two people may have the same name and surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look on the -- yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then also under Roman II, the second heading, "Employees in the Iron Ore Mine," I said I know number 10, Branko Kicema; number 11, Milorad Stakic; number 18, Cedo Vuleta; Branko Rosic, number 21; Dragomir Mamuza, number 26, I know him too. Maybe some others but it's hard to remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the people who are listed as caterers cooks, butchers, and food drivers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Delic, I know him, number 1; I know Novak Ratkovic, known as Novo, number 2; number 5, Krstan Zavasic, I know him; and number 7, Pero Rendic, I know him; I also know number 8, Ranko Radanovic; number 9, Milan Andic; number 10, Vinka Andzic, handwritten, I know her too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the numbers that you don't off the top of your head recognise, the names Dervida or Seva, you just may not have come across them or you didn't know their names? Is that, perhaps, a possibility, that you just didn't know their names? Maybe a face but not a name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the people whose names appear here are associated with the same Omarska Police Station which was your station and which had its functions transferred to Omarska camp for that period of time. It's the same police station we're talking about, is it not, your station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it different? It says "Wartime Police Station Omarska" and then it describes these people. What is your understanding of the use of the term "Wartime Police Station"? It's at the top, above the date of 21st June.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "station of the wartime police" or "of the reserve police" was a term frequently used, and it is a separate entity. And on this list there is not a single person from the Omarska Police Station department. This is some kind of preparation for a wartime police, a list of workers engaged to secure the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it appear to be that they were, as it were, support staff for the work of your police station, the Omarska Police Station, in their work at the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that some of them -- no, actually, it is not possible because none of these people were employed in the Omarska Police Station because it says under headings, "Member of the army, employees in the mines, employees for the food department." So the purpose of this document is quite clear. None of these people were working in the Omarska Police Station department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not physically, that would be understandable, but working in support of the work of the Omarska Department in the camp? Would that be your understanding based on the types of names and the descriptions of the functions here? Vuleta for example, came in here. I think you were going to have Pero Rendic at one point, Milan Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not helping out the police station department in Omarska. They were not helping them out in any way or supporting them. Some of these people that I know were employed in the camp in various areas. Therefore, their link with the police station department does not exist. There is a link between them and the camp because Zoran Delic was the cook in the camp, and some of these, like Branko Kicema, Milorad Stakic, were drivers in the iron ore mine, and I don't exclude them being linked to the work of the camp. What I am excluding is them being linked to the work of the Omarska Police Station department. Because you see Ranko Radanovic, commander of the regional war staff, Omarska, I don't know what he's doing on that list. The purpose of this list is to issue passes, as far as I can see. So to be the commander of the regional staff, Omarska; Andzic, assistant commander for logistics, somebody is asking that these people be issued passes. So these people have nothing to do with the police station department. But regarding work in the investigation centre or the camp, that is possible because I know some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Having helped us link up their relationship to the work of the camp, where would the passes come from? Would they come from your police station as the station in charge of security at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that they have passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What it says, Mr. Kvocka, if you look at the top, it says list, the very heading underneath the date, "List of persons" -- I'm sorry, "of workers providing security for the Omarska Collection Centre who need to be issued special passes." Do you see that, Mr. Kvocka? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was just going to say that it is clear from this that somebody is asking for passes for some people, but I don't see to whom they are addressing this request. That person has just drawn up a list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would the police station be the normal issuing agency for passes in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly the Public Security Station in Prijedor, which would mean the entity superior to the police station in Prijedor, because the police station in Prijedor itself could not issue such passes, as far as I know. It could also have been the Crisis Staff. You are asking me something beyond my field of knowledge. It could have been the Crisis Staff, even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, allow me to interrupt you. Mr. Kvocka, looking at this document, the last paragraph, could you tell me - I have the English version, not the French version - what does it mean, [In English] "Police employees organised in three shifts and for whom regular records are kept"? What are these police employees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can understand this, it refers to the security employees and others because it says all others entering the collection centre compound will be police employees, organised into three shifts, and for whom regular records are kept. So this refers to members of the police who do not need passes. They have official IDs. That is what this refers to, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Continue, Ms. Susan Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that include you, Mr. Kvocka, as a person who would fit into this paragraph that Judge Rodrigues just asked you about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have any special pass; I had my official ID as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The signature on this document is indicated as -- it's a translation, of course, but the signature on the Serbo-Croat document purports to be that of Zeljko Meakic, and if he is writing it and --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- if he is using a term "wartime police station, Omarska," did he discuss the use of that term with you, he as the commander of that station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In those days, I wasn't even around. Well, the list was drafted on the 21st of June by him, but when he signed it on the 29th of June, it was not possible for us to discuss it because I was no longer there. And he had no reason to talk about it with me. I don't understand the implication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were discussing other --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just add? In my opinion, someone gave him -- ordered him to make a list of persons for whom some type of passes were required to be able to enter, and then he drew up this list. That is my explanation for this list. And then he passed on this list to whoever had asked him to compile it, and then when they prepared those passes, it says here that he collected them on the 29th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that helpful explanation. The thing that I was actually trying to understand was this term "wartime police station," and perhaps you do not know of its use. I wanted to ask you, we were discussing various camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher could distribute, please, 3/204.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the term "wartime reserve police station," but in theory. So both terms were used, either where wartime police or reserve police in free speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wartime police station would also be the same as reserve police station in this war-like time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could happen that people had the same thing in mind. Some would describe it as wartime and someone else as reserve, but according to the regulations, as far as I know, it can become a wartime situation only once a declaration of war has been issued. I'm not sure about that, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at a document dated 28th of July, 1992. This document is entitled -- and it says "Omarska SC" which is -- is a bracketed collection centre. This document is a list of first category persons. Have you in the course of your time in Omarska -- I realise we're looking at a July document, but in the course of your time there, have you seen lists like this categorising persons, a physical list like this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw it some time ago. I don't know whether it was the same, the same list, but a list of persons sent to Manjaca by category among the documents that you yourself disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this list, Mr. Kvocka, if we run down to number six, the name, the name Edna Dautovic, this --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- person was in Omarska camp. Do you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but from all the testimony that I heard here, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm almost certain that she was there. I do not know her personally. I didn't notice her under that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, perhaps, in the course of the testimony in this trial that Edna Dautovic's body was found in a cave in the summer of 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Your investigator, I think, testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going down the list, looking at number 43, the name (redacted) (redacted), this person also was in Omarska, and do you know anything about his condition while he was there, anything about his dates of departure, whether or not he was a person who allegedly suffered difficult handling at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard while I was there that (redacted), was among the detainees. Probably because of his father and certain characteristics of his, his name was mentioned. So I heard it, though I did not personally ever see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 46, (redacted), do you recall testimony that her body was found in a cave in the summer of 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember when the gentleman was speaking here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to number 95, Emir Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall testimony that this individual was severely beaten while in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to number 98 -- oh, by the way, the Beganovic individual, this is the person whose mother was in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found her there on two or three occasions, and according to what my wife told me and my mother-in-law, they were almost inseparable for a month, either in my apartment or in the house of my wife's family, because of the events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hajra Hadzic, number 98, do you recall testimony that she was the only woman to have been in the "white house," and she has disappeared, never to have been heard from or seen again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this part of the testimony, that she was in the "white house." I never saw her there; that is, I never saw anyone in the "white house." I never entered the place. I cannot remember what the exact testimony about her disappearance was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your witness, Mrs. Markovski, Markovska, who was here last week spoke about first category witnesses. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
