utterances.text: Did you have any input in determining who would end up in a first category witness list?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer your question. I don't think that there are -- that there is any information which would link me to that. I never saw any kind of list during my stay there. No, not a single list. No list whatsoever did I see. From time to time I would see a list of two or three persons who were taken into custody in Prijedor and brought over there. This falls within the scope of work of the staff, that is, of the three members of the staff, and the inspectors, that is, who determined the categories and according to what criteria. I really don't know anything about that. I know that there were stories about the existence of some categories amongst the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to inform the Chamber, there is an error that has great significance. It looks like page 90, line 25, it said: "Did you have input in determining who would end up in a first category prisoner list," and it came down -- I'm sorry. It may have been my error. It should have been "prisoner list" and I think I may have spoken "witness list" and it's not -- it was my error. I don't know how the term "witness" crawled into my vocabulary there. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know why Hajra Hodzic was in the "white house," even though you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, may I just ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain my objection? Once again, I have to apologise for intervening. Ms. Markovska made an explicit statement here, she said that any one member of the personnel staff never took part in that work. Mr. Kvocka said a moment ago that he didn't know Hajra Hodzic, that he never actually entered the "white house," and now we have the question, "Do you know why Hajra Hodzic was in the 'white house'?" I really have to intervene, Your Honours. I am perfectly aware of everything you said and I fully support your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to Madam Judge Wald in a moment. Mr. Simic, your logic doesn't seem to be complete. Mr. Kvocka, it is possible that he has never actually entered the "white house"; however, it is possible that he knows about things that took place there because somebody may have told him about that. You cannot say that the counsel cannot ask Mr. Kvocka whether he knew what was happening just because he at one point said that he never entered the premises of the "white house." I really don't see the reason for your objection, Mr. Simic. I think that it is a perfectly reasonable question, that is, the question, do you know what was happening in the "white house," although he said that he had never entered the "white house." MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to respond, I fully agree with what you said. However, there was a question here which is really out of place. The question read, "Do you know who put Hajra Hodzic in the 'white house,'" and Mr. Kvocka said that he didn't know the person, that he had never seen the person. So I'm talking about a very specific question here, not a general matter. Otherwise, I fully agree with what you stated in this respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just needed some edification. I understand that you are not, at the present moment, seeking to admit this list. But in terms of a fact-finder, since you did go down the list and question Mr. Kvocka about it, for my edification, and since it has no signature by anybody or anything that I know about, could you just tell me a little bit about where it came from?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, gladly. This was in the list of what is known as Prijedor documents. There were search warrants executed in various institutions in Prijedor municipality in, I believe, late 1997 or -- there were several so I want to be sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't even need to know the date. I just want to know where. It doesn't have any kind of markings on it that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is not uncommon, Your Honour. Documents are sometimes found just as lists. But the source was from the institutions of Prijedor themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You don't know which institution this one came out of?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can get what's called the identification form and try to give you as -- identify which one from that. It would not be on the body of this document. It would be separate. I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to let Judge Rodrigues know on this, the question was, do you know why Hajra Hodzic was in the "white house," and that was what the record reflected. I wonder if I might proceed with that question, if the Chamber would permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can ask the question, we will get the answer, and I will have some clarification to ask afterwards. But would you please start with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Hajra Hodzic, a woman, was in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to respond a moment ago but then this discussion started. I already stated that I didn't know at all whether she was in the "white house" or not. I never noticed any woman in the "white house." I never noticed any people in the "white house." I know that there were detainees there, in the "white house," but I don't know whether there was any woman there, and I never saw that. So she may have been there but maybe she was not there. So I cannot tell you anything about why she was there if I don't know whether she was there or not. It's very difficult for me to answer your question. She was there probably because someone had sent her there. Then we can go on and speculate as to why someone had sent her there, and then maybe because the person in question thought that she was guilty of something, and then we can go on and on like this forever. I apologise, but I really cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you something, Mr. Kvocka, at this point. You told us that you had never seen this list. I thought that the question was if you had ever heard anyone speak about this list. I didn't have an opportunity to quote your exact words because a discussion followed, as you have stated. However, I observed something. You said the following: [In English] "... said persons were being put in different categories."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give us some more explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories, Your Honour, circulating amongst the guards. But I believe that it was a day or two days before I left that people started speaking about some categories of those who were being interrogated, that is, that some kind of categories existed. Whether it was A, B, and C or number 1, 2, or 3, I think that they used both terms, and nothing else, nothing specific, as to why some individuals were in this category and others in some other category. Momcilo Gruban, named Ckalja, once called me in Prijedor and informed me about his concerns about one of my brothers-in-law. He didn't want to say directly to me what it was all about, but he thought that he might be in one of the categories of the people who were supposed to go to Manjaca. So if I analyse all that and if I have in mind what I heard in the camp, that would be all the knowledge that I have about such categories or groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember, more or less, when you heard about those lists for the first time? Despite the fact that they were very vague and not very specific, but do you remember when was the first time that you heard about such lists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After four or five days after the opening of the centre, a number of people were released. At that time one of the inspectors, maybe Rajko Mijic, said, "This category can go home." So that was the kind of context in which the word "category" was used. So that was the first time that I knew about it, that I learned about it. But then there was a period of time when no mention was made of any such categories. And then the next time - it was during that period of time which preceded my departure, that is, before I left - I heard people speak about some categories, categories of people who were to go to Manjaca, those who were to go to Trnopolje, and those who were to be released and sent home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that first time that you heard about it would have been four days after the opening of the camp, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe even six or seven. I cannot be more specific than that. On that occasion, two buses of people were taken to Puharska. I know that from some people who were there, that is, that those people were from that area. They were all taken to Prijedor and then taken back to their neighbourhood, which is called Gornja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, is there a connection between the results of the work of the investigators and the production of such lists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think all of those people were interrogated, and such were the options in discussions, that people would be released in groups once interrogations were completed. I no longer remember the date, but at one point in time, that practice stopped. Inspectors would, from time to time, take away people individually in their buses. But I don't know when it was exactly, around the 10th, the 12th, or the 13th, when that practice stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Simic wanted to say something, wanted to react? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just for the record, I think we have a problem here. Once again, something is missing as regards when Kvocka learned about the existence of such groups. He was referring to the period of time when he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that. Maybe not in English, but I heard that part. I think that we have a lot of problems here. It is very difficult for us to say that this or that was explicitly said during the hearing. I think that the previous session was finished at two minutes past one and the record said nine minutes past one so I know that it was not correct. If I read the record and I know enough English, sometimes I can also spot some mistakes. But of course, I can follow everything in French. We are coming back to this problem of translation. As you know, there is an adage, a Latin proverb, for those who still remember Latin from school, which says "tradutore traditore." A translator is a traitor, that is the saying. So when we are translating, there's always something that is omitted, that is dropped out, and those are the conditions we are working in. We can't be absolutely perfect. Let me say something else. All of you know what hearsay testimony is, that is, a passing on of information from one person to another in a chain and then the information is lost or, rather, is transformed and modified. But we must recognise that we are working under such conditions of human beings. I am no god, and I don't think that we're all angels, so we are working under normal human conditions. I myself heard it, but I can ask Mr. Kvocka once again. What did you say, Mr. Kvocka, that you heard about this, above all, after you had left the camp? What did you hear that was being said for the first time then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very end of my stay there, there were some stories about the categorisation of detainees. Anything more than that is something that I heard once I had left, especially from this gentleman, Mr. Gruban, who told me that there were three categories and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Now we can link it up to what we heard. Do we find it in the English transcript now? Yes, fine. You may continue for another five minutes, Ms. Susan Somers, only.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Susan Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions for -- I'm sorry. I'm aware of the time, and I shall just ask two more questions now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Momcilo Gruban called you about your brother-in-law, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, really. I was a bit worried. He said that he had heard stories that he may, perhaps, be sent to Manjaca. That was all. After that I was worried. But, of course, I wasn't pleased or indifferent. I don't know how to explain it. I felt there was nothing else I could do. However, afterwards he informed me that that was not the case, that this was information that he had heard and that he was in Trnopolje. Actually, he informed me that they were in Trnopolje, and then I took certain steps to get them out of the Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which brother-in-law was he speaking about? What's the name, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad. Actually, the one that was said to have participated in certain guard duty prior to these events. So that I can think about it and make my own conclusions, he probably said that to the inspectors and then this followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If these categories dealt with the end of the time of Omarska camp, would you know what happened to the prisoners who were neither sent to Manjaca nor to Trnopolje nor home? What happened to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. Whether there were any such people who were not sent anywhere at the very end, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time to break for the day? I can ask more questions, but they will take us to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, do you have an estimate of the time you still need to complete your cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This had come up earlier today and I had made a guesstimate. I would hope to finish by the end of the morning session. I have tried to -- in light of a concern that was raised about time, I'd like to try to finish by the morning session's end, by the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do not forget, Ms. Susan Somers - maybe now is not the time to say that - but don't forget that you have documents to tender in connection with, I think, the last witness prior to Mr. Kvocka. We can deal with that at the end of the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka, with all the documents. Do you understand? Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tomorrow we will meet again at twenty past nine here in the same courtroom. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise for raising this matter at the very end, but I think it is a good moment for us to follow on from what Her Honour Judge Wald said. At the very beginning when we mentioned the first documents, I asked where they came from. They are given to us in copies. Many of them are untranslated. Please look at the one you have in front of you. You have a black blot in the Serbian language version and something written here. In your language, you don't see that at all. I'm also listening to the French interpretation as you. The differences are considerable. We keep hearing "poste de station de police" in French, or department of the "poste de police," and in English it is always post [as interpreted] the police, so I do apologise to the Chamber for taking up time. Ms. Somers should give us with the document every time an indication of where it came from so that we can at least here in the courtroom look at the original, because I have written a letter to Ms. Somers requesting this and this was refused. And we can raise that matter at the Status Conference, but I don't want to keep you any longer. This is a piece of paper without any signature, that somebody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wrote someplace, maybe yesterday, but I have every respect for my learned friend. I know that that is not so, and that it was found where Ms. Somers tells us it was found. But we cannot behave in a proper manner as professionals unless we have evidence that that is so. Thank you very much, and I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. I myself have tried to look to see what is written in the original, and it says, "Omarska, Category 1." We don't need to translate that, but Ms. Susan Somers, could you respond to this concern of Mr. Fila's?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God knows what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about 3/204.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I am referring to the document that was just shown to the witness. There's something scribbled by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and what I see here it says, "Omarska, Category 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I have a different document than you. So Ms. Susan Somers, you have heard the concerns. Are you prepared to respond to them, or do you wish to respond on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can briefly indicate that in terms of the request that Mr. Fila addressed to me, that I spoke of Mr. Jovanovic about, and I think perhaps Mr. Fila has his information incorrect, but that's handled right now inter partes, as the Court wishes us to do, before any motions are filed. We are in the process of trying to, we are in the process of trying to get the information sufficient to honour his request. On any possibly extraneous markings, unless it was done -- and I cannot give you -- I'm giving you an off-the-cuff, sort of prosecutorial observation, perhaps in the course of indexing the document, it looks like someone may have written "Omarska, Category 1" in English. We can see if that may have come in with that indication as it -- I am sure it was erroneously done, but it could have happened. It clearly is an English spelling of "category," so it looks like that is it. But in answer to Her Honour Judge Wald's inquiry, I can check the informational document that gives the location of seizure, and if that would be of some help, I will do that for both documents that we discussed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the question is, Ms. Susan Somers, I think, that you must give that information to the Defence so that the Defence should have an idea about the authenticity because as far as I know, you're showing the document for the first time now to the Defence, and the Defence needs to have that information. Otherwise, as Mr. Fila said, one could imagine that this document was drawn up yesterday somewhere. So this is a question of authenticity that we are raising here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What I can do so as to avoid my own getting involved in testifying, to -- if the Chamber would accept this as a kind of an ad hoc explanation practice, is when I ask about a document, if it's not objectionable, I can say a document located in such and such a location from the Prijedor collection, if that would be helpful. It's a bit awkward because I'm not testifying, but I could put that in; otherwise, there can -- if authenticity is an issue, then -- I'm sorry. I'm just reminded that some documents from the Prijedor collection were also tendered by the Defence, D40/1, so it may come up running two ways. But I can at least indicate to the Chamber so it has enough of an idea, and I think it would be helpful to Defence counsel, if the Chamber will permit me that way. Otherwise, I would have to have an investigator come in with a list of documents and indicate the source from the warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just say what would be satisfactory to me, because a document like this, and many of them, a birth certificate, a death certificate, you're not going to get too excited about if they've got some evidence of authenticity in it. But this is a fairly important document, and I think even though you -- to give it credence, at least, I would need to know where it was taken from, when it was taken approximately, you know, and a signature. It could be, I suppose, by affidavit. I mean, it could be by affidavit or something, that this was in the group of things seized in the Prijedor, I'm using just a -- police station, you know, pursuant to a search warrant on March 1st, 1999, signed by a real name. I mean, if -- it's just too much to sort of have a document there --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- that doesn't have any ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask you, Judge Wald, and Your Honours, would the Chamber prefer that we take note of these documents, that I simply tender them, and then at the end have an affidavit so that we don't have a repeat presentation or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: For me, whatever -- so long as at some point, the thing is identified in some way so that I know that it wasn't, in fact, something somebody decided on the last day --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If that's okay with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is a question of interest to the Defence as well because we are in a system when documents are exchanged between the parties, and the Judges have nothing to do with the game. But that is not true, I think. Each one of us often places himself in the perspective of the legal system he comes from. I think this is a matter you have to regulate with the Defence. I personally am satisfied, but I don't know whether Defence is satisfied. And that is why I suggested from the beginning -- I know very often that one party doesn't like the other party to know in advance. It's strategy; that is a game. But that is why I said show your documents, discuss questions of authenticity, and afterwards we'll see. I don't want to enlarge the debate, but I think there was an orientation that we took the other day during the Status Conference to see whether admissibility comes before authenticity or not. In my view, I think that was the intervention of Mr. O'Sullivan, along those lines, if I'm not wrong. But in my opinion, we have to address the question of authenticity first, and then see its relevance and admit it. And after it is admitted, it can be distributed. How can we admit a document if we doubt its authenticity? If you look at Rule 65 ter when there is reference to the exhibits, either from the Prosecution, that is paragraph (E), or from the Defence, paragraph (G) I think, whenever exhibits are mentioned, it has to -- we have to be sure that there is no objection as to authenticity of the other party. The Defence has to produce a list of exhibits with the opinion of the Prosecution regarding authenticity. I mean, authenticity is the first thing that we have to address. So now, Ms. Susan Somers, why are we talking about this document if we're still doubting its authenticity? First authenticity has to be resolved, and then only afterwards can the document be used. Or, if that was not possible in advance, I submit the document in the courtroom saying this document comes from such and such a source, it was obtained in such and such a way, and we have it here. And after that, we see if we believe what you are saying. But when you say in that way, "I will be testifying," we also know that a document speaks for itself. The question is, is it authentic or not, because afterwards the document speaks for itself. So I think you realise what the issue is. We can have that discussion next week, perhaps, but at this stage when presenting a document at the hearing, you have to authenticate it, telling us what the source is, where it comes from, and so on. But we can't go on much longer; otherwise, we'll go on forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, just one sentence. If something is written on that document in English, you will believe me that they can't even speak B/C/S over there, never mind English, so it's no longer an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a possible interpretation. That is also one I share. It is certainly not the person who typed out this document who thought about it and said "category 1" in English. No, somebody was working with this document, an English-speaking person, and who wrote down this category 1. So, Ms. Susan Somers, there is, to say the least, confusion. Use the document, yes, but once we have -- we all share the authenticity of that document. What the document says is something else. If I go on, the interpreters are really going to call me a traitor, so I think we'll end there and we will meet again tomorrow at 9.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
